\titlefont   MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution

MemTensor Team
Abstract

Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately 1.86×1.86\times end-to-end inference speedup and a 66×66\times reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

1 Introduction

The rapid evolution of foundation models is expanding the boundary of what can be natively learned and performed within a single model. Many capabilities are progressively internalized from external systems into the model itself, such as reasoning [1, 2] and multimodality [3, 4]. Memory represents another fundamental capability, enabling models to accumulate experience and adapt over extended interactions [5, 6]. Our previous work, Metis [7], first introduced memory foundation models to internalize memory as a native capability of foundation models. This offers a path beyond external context and enables models to continuously accumulate information and experience, which marks a critical step towards memory-native evolution.

To improve memory capabilities, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture with substantial upgrades over Metis, while retaining the structure of dynamic local memory and trainable hyper memory. It replaces token selection with a stable token-level update mechanism based on Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) [8]. To further scale native memory capability, we introduce Mixture-of-Storage (MoS) to expand the capacity of native memory. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano with 36B parameters (3B activated, 10M dynamic memory) and MemT-1.0-Flash with 288B parameters (17B activated, 336M dynamic memory).

Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline for MemT-1.0. The first stage performs continued pre-training (CPT) to establish language modeling capabilities with native memory [9]. The post-training stage further adapts the model to downstream memory tasks while preserving its general capabilities [10]. To support this training pipeline, we construct a large-scale dataset of 34B tokens. Across 11 memory benchmarks, our models outperform parametric memory baselines on average, showing effective utilization of historical information without accessing the original context during inference. They also largely preserve general capabilities under the noise setting. Our evaluation shows an increasing end-to-end inference latency and storage overhead advantage over full context on longer histories.

To support training and deployment, we develop a distributed infrastructure, which preserves memory isolation across independent trajectories. We organize stateful inference around separate memory storage and utilization procedures, with shared model parameters and trajectory-specific memory states. For a fixed memory configuration, the persistent state size remains constant as interactions accumulate. In addition, we explore the scaling behavior of MemT-1.0. Unlike general foundation models [11], memory foundation models introduce memory capacity as a critical scaling dimension, so we conduct scaling studies over memory capacity and training data. These findings provide valuable guidance for building stronger memory foundation models.

We further apply MemT-1.0 to experience-guided coding agents, where retrieved procedural experience is internalized into native memory to guide subsequent actions. On SWE-bench Verified [12] and SWE-bench Multilingual [13], our method improves average task success and consistency across repeated runs over agents without experience, while achieving performance comparable to explicit textual experience. These findings extend the role of native memory from information recall to procedural guidance in multi-step execution.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
∙\bullet We introduce MemT-1.0, a memory foundation model architecture with improved memory storage and utilization mechanisms, together with MoS for scalable memory capacity.
∙\bullet Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we design a two-stage training pipeline including CPT and post-training stages, with a corresponding infrastructure design. We construct a training corpus of 34B tokens, and systematically evaluate MemT-1.0 on both memory and general benchmarks. The results show that MemT-1.0 achieves superior memory performance while largely preserving general capabilities.
∙\bullet We explore the scaling behavior of memory capabilities in MemT-1.0. We further deploy MemT-1.0 in practical agentic coding tasks to demonstrate its effectiveness and potential in enabling memory-native evolution. We also discuss its current limitations and promising directions for future development.

2 Model Architecture

2.1 Overview

MemT-1.0 is formulated under a multi-step scenario with discrete steps t∈{1,2,⋯,T}t\in\{1,2,\cdots,T\}, as presented in Figure 4. At step tt, let θt\theta_{t} denote the current model parameters. Given the input XtX_{t}, the autoregressive generation process can be formulated as

yt,k∼P(⋅|Xt,Yt,<k;θt),y_{t,k}\sim P\left(\cdot|X_{t},Y_{t,<k};\theta_{t}\right),

where Yt,<kY_{t,<k} denotes the tokens generated before yt,ky_{t,k}. Meanwhile, the stateful model parameter is updated by

θt+1∼P(⋅|Xt,Yt;θt),\theta_{t+1}\sim P\left(\cdot|X_{t},Y_{t};\theta_{t}\right),

where YtY_{t} is all generated tokens at step tt. MemT-1.0 is built upon general causal language models. We denote the input sequence as St,k=Xt||Yt,<k=(xt,1,⋯,yt,1,⋯,yt,k−1)S_{t,k}=X_{t}||Y_{t,<k}=\left(x_{t,1},\cdots,y_{t,1},\cdots,y_{t,k-1}\right) with length Lt,kL_{t,k}. First, the input is mapped to the initial hidden state 𝐇t,k(0)∈ℝLt,k×d\mathbf{H}^{(0)}_{t,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{t,k}\times d} through the embedding layer, where dd is the dimension of the hidden state. Then, it is processed sequentially by LL stacked Transformer blocks [14] as follows:

𝐇t,k(l)=TransformerBlock⁡(𝐇t,k(l−1)),for l=1,2,⋯L.\mathbf{H}^{(l)}_{t,k}=\operatorname{TransformerBlock}\left(\mathbf{H}^{(l-1)}_{t,k}\right),\quad\text{for $l=1,2,\cdots L$}.

After that, the last hidden state 𝐇t,k(L)\mathbf{H}^{(L)}_{t,k} is normalized and projected into the vocabulary space through the language modeling head 𝐖LM∈ℝd×|𝒱|\mathbf{W}_{\text{LM}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|\mathcal{V}|}, and a softmax function is then applied to obtain the probability distribution by

P(⋅|Xt,Yt,<k;θt)=Softmax(Norm(𝐡t,k(L))𝐖LM),P\left(\cdot|X_{t},Y_{t,<k};\theta_{t}\right)=\Softmax\left(\Norm\left(\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t,k}\right)\mathbf{W}_{\text{LM}}\right),

where |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| is the vocabulary size and 𝐡t,k(L)\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t,k} is the last position of 𝐇t,k(L)\mathbf{H}^{(L)}_{t,k}.

MemT-1.0 augments each selected standard Transformer block with a native memory block, which is responsible for maintaining the memory from previous information. For the ll-th Transformer block, we denote the computation of attention output as

𝐀ori,t,k(l)=Attention⁡(𝐇~t,k(l)),𝐇~t,k(l)=Pre−Attention⁡(𝐇t,k(l−1)),\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{\text{ori},t,k}=\operatorname{Attention}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t,k}\right),\quad\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t,k}=\operatorname{Pre-Attention}\left({\mathbf{H}}^{(l-1)}_{t,k}\right),

where Attention⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Attention}\left(\cdot\right) represents the backbone attention and 𝐇~(l)\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)} indicates the hidden state after pre-attention operations, such as pre-normalization. MemT-1.0 introduces a parallel memory attention mechanism to utilize the parametric memory accumulated from previous steps for targeted layers, by

𝐀t,k(l)=𝐀ori,t,k(l)+𝐀mem,t,k(l),𝐀mem,t,k(l)=MemoryAttention⁡(𝐇~t,k(l),⋅),\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{t,k}=\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{\text{ori},t,k}+\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{\text{mem},t,k},\quad\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{\text{mem},t,k}=\operatorname{MemoryAttention}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t,k};\cdot\right),

where 𝐀mem,t,k(l)\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{\text{mem},t,k} indicates the output of memory attention. After that, the combined attention output 𝐀t,k(l)\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{t,k} is used in the subsequent computation as

𝐇t,k(l)=Post−Attention⁡(𝐀t,k(l),𝐇t,k(l−1)).\mathbf{H}^{(l)}_{t,k}=\operatorname{Post-Attention}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{t,k},{\mathbf{H}}^{(l-1)}_{t,k}\right).

For different backbones, we preserve the original Pre−Attention⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Pre-Attention}\left(\cdot\right), Attention⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Attention}\left(\cdot\right), and Post−Attention⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Post-Attention}\left(\cdot\right) unchanged to retain the backbone capabilities, and introduce memory through MemoryAttention⁡(⋅)\operatorname{MemoryAttention}\left(\cdot\right) for different backbones. Specifically, we use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [15], as released, as the backbone of MemT-1.0-Nano and a further post-trained DeepSeek-V4-Flash [16] (Section 3.1) as the backbone of MemT-1.0-Flash.

2.2 Native Memory Block

2.2.1 Native Memory State

Following our previous work Metis [7], a native memory block in MemT-1.0 comprises a local memory block and a hyper memory block. The former stores online information, while the latter is trained to equip general foundation models with memory capabilities in a data-driven manner.

Local Memory Block. In MemT-1.0, the dynamic memory state at the tt-th step and ll-th layer can be represented as 𝐌t(l)∈ℝHk​v×dk×dv\mathbf{M}_{t}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{kv}\times d_{k}\times d_{v}}, where dk,dvd_{k},d_{v} represent the dimensions of memory keys and values, and Hk​vH_{kv} denotes the number of memory channels. Compared with Metis, we remove the query-key normalization vector and extend the memory state to multiple channels. We initialize 𝐌t(l)=𝟎\mathbf{M}_{t}^{(l)}=\mathbf{0} at the start of new trajectories.

Hyper Memory Block. In the hyper memory block, the multi-channel projections of memory query, key, and value are denoted as 𝐖~Q(l)∈ℝHq×d×dk\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{Q}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{q}\times d\times d_{k}}, 𝐖~K(l)∈ℝHk​v×d×dk\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{K}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{kv}\times d\times d_{k}} and 𝐖~V(l)∈ℝHk​v×d×dv\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{V}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{kv}\times d\times d_{v}} for each layer ll. Beyond these core memory projections, this block includes all other trainable parameters for memory processing. First, the gating projections include the erase gate 𝐖β(l)∈ℝd×Hk​v×dk\mathbf{W}_{\beta}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times H_{kv}\times d_{k}} and the write gate 𝐖ω(l)∈ℝd×Hk​v×dv\mathbf{W}_{\omega}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times H_{kv}\times d_{v}}, along with the forget gate components consisting of 𝐖f(l)∈ℝd×dgate\mathbf{W}_{f}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\text{gate}}}, 𝐖λ(l)∈ℝdgate×Hk​v×dk\mathbf{W}_{\lambda}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{gate}}\times H_{kv}\times d_{k}}, 𝐛λ(l)∈ℝHk​v×dk\mathbf{b}_{\lambda}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{kv}\times d_{k}}, and a learnable vector 𝐬(l)∈ℝHk​v\mathbf{s}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{kv}}. Finally, the memory output gating is parameterized by a shared down-projection 𝐖g/d(l)∈ℝd×dg/d\mathbf{W}_{g/d}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{g/d}} and a multi-channel up-projection 𝐖g/u(l)∈ℝHq×dg/d×dv\mathbf{W}_{g/u}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{q}\times d_{g/d}\times d_{v}}. Generally, we have Hq=Hk​vH_{q}=H_{kv} to align query channel and key-value channels. These trainable parameters are denoted as ϕ\phi, which can be optimized during the training phase and remain fixed during online interaction.

In summary, the model parameters θt\theta_{t} at step tt include the backbone parameters θb\theta_{b}, the static but trainable parameters ϕ\phi, and the dynamic memory states {𝐌t(l)}l=1L\{\mathbf{M}_{t}^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L}. During online inference, these dynamic memory states are responsible for storing online information and evolve over interactions.

2.2.2 Native Memory Procedures

MemT-1.0 consists of two parallel native procedures, including memory storage and memory utilization. The memory storage procedure updates the dynamic memory states to preserve information from the current interaction, while the memory utilization procedure retrieves information from previously accumulated memory states to support autoregressive generation.

Native Memory Storage Procedure. MemT-1.0 replaces the token selection with a stable token-level update mechanism based on GDN-2 [8] to update the dynamic memory state in each turn. As the memory storage procedure is triggered at the turn level, we denote the hidden states as 𝐇t(l)\mathbf{H}^{(l)}_{t} of St=Xt||YtS_{t}=X_{t}||Y_{t}. For the pre-attention input 𝐇~t(l)\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}, we compute the memory key and value of the hh-th channel by

𝐊t,h(l)=L2Norm⁡(𝐇~t(l)​𝐖~K,h(l)),𝐕t,h(l)=𝐇~t(l)​𝐖~V,h(l),\mathbf{K}_{t,h}^{(l)}=\operatorname{L2Norm}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{K,h}^{(l)}\right),\quad\mathbf{V}_{t,h}^{(l)}=\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{V,h}^{(l)},

where 𝐖~K,h(l)\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{K,h}^{(l)} and 𝐖~V,h(l)\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{V,h}^{(l)} are the key and value projection matrices for the hh-th memory channel. Then, the erase gate and write gate can be obtained by

𝜷t(l)=σ⁡(𝐇~t(l)​𝐖β(l)),𝝎t(l)=σ⁡(𝐇~t(l)​𝐖ω(l)),\bm{\beta}_{t}^{(l)}=\sigma\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\mathbf{W}_{\beta}^{(l)}\right),\quad\bm{\omega}_{t}^{(l)}=\sigma\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\mathbf{W}_{\omega}^{(l)}\right),

where 𝐖β(l),𝐖ω(l)\mathbf{W}_{\beta}^{(l)},\mathbf{W}_{\omega}^{(l)} are gating projection matrices. In addition, the forget gate is calculated by

𝝀t,h(l)=−exp(𝐬h(l))⊙Softplus(𝐅t(l)𝐖λ,h(l)+𝐛λ,h(l)),𝐅t(l)=𝐇~t(l)𝐖f(l),\bm{\lambda}_{t,h}^{(l)}=-\exp\left(\mathbf{s}^{(l)}_{h}\right)\odot\operatorname{Softplus}\left(\mathbf{F}_{t}^{(l)}\mathbf{W}_{\lambda,h}^{(l)}+\mathbf{b}_{\lambda,h}^{(l)}\right),\quad\mathbf{F}_{t}^{(l)}=\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\mathbf{W}_{f}^{(l)},

where 𝐖f(l),𝐖λ(l),𝐛λ(l),𝐬h(l)\mathbf{W}_{f}^{(l)},\mathbf{W}_{\lambda}^{(l)},\mathbf{b}_{\lambda}^{(l)},\mathbf{s}_{h}^{(l)} are forget-gate parameters. To prevent the divergence of memory states during updates, we introduce a stable mechanism for the token-level update, where it first calculates

𝐔t,i(l)=𝜷t,i(l)⊙𝐊t,i(l).\mathbf{U}_{t,i}^{(l)}=\sqrt{\bm{\beta}_{t,i}^{(l)}}\odot\mathbf{K}_{t,i}^{(l)}.

Then, the memory state can be updated by

𝐌~t,i,h(l)=[𝐈−𝐔t,i,h(l)⊤​𝐔t,i,h(l)]⋅𝐃t,i,h(l)​𝐌~t,i−1,h(l)+𝐔t,i,h(l)⊤​(𝝎t,i,h(l)⊙𝐕t,i,h(l)),\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}=\left[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{U}_{t,i,h}^{(l)\top}\mathbf{U}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\right]\cdot\mathbf{D}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,i-1,h}^{(l)}+\mathbf{U}_{t,i,h}^{(l)\top}\left(\bm{\omega}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\odot\mathbf{V}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\right),

where the initialization is given by 𝐌~t,0,h(l)=𝐌t,h(l)\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,0,h}^{(l)}=\mathbf{M}_{t,h}^{(l)}, and the state transition is defined as 𝐌t+1,h(l)=𝐌~t,Lt,h(l)\mathbf{M}_{t+1,h}^{(l)}=\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,L_{t},h}^{(l)}, with

𝐃t,i,h(l)=Diag⁡[exp⁡(𝝀t,i,h(l))].\mathbf{D}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}=\operatorname{Diag}\left[\exp\left(\bm{\lambda}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\right)\right].

The detailed analysis of our stable mechanism on GDN-2 is presented in Appendix C.

Native Memory Utilization Procedure. In MemT-1.0, we remove the key-value normalization from Metis. Because the memory utilization operates at the token level in parallel, we omit the decoding index kk for simplicity. For the step tt, we read out information from the current memory state 𝐌t,h(l)\mathbf{M}_{t,h}^{(l)} by

𝐑t,h(l)=𝐐t,h(l)​𝐌t,h(l)dk,𝐐t,h(l)=L2Norm⁡(𝐇~t(l)​𝐖~Q,h(l)),\mathbf{R}_{t,h}^{(l)}=\frac{\mathbf{Q}_{t,h}^{(l)}\mathbf{M}_{t,h}^{(l)}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}},\quad\mathbf{Q}_{t,h}^{(l)}=\operatorname{L2Norm}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{Q,h}^{(l)}\right),

where 𝐖~Q,h(l)\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{Q,h}^{(l)} is the memory query projection matrix. After that, we calculate the memory output gate by

𝐆t,h(l)=𝐇~t(l)​𝐖g/d(l)​𝐖g/u,h(l),\mathbf{G}_{t,h}^{(l)}=\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t}\mathbf{W}_{g/d}^{(l)}\mathbf{W}_{g/u,h}^{(l)},

where 𝐖g/d(l),𝐖g/u,h(l)\mathbf{W}_{g/d}^{(l)},\mathbf{W}_{g/u,h}^{(l)} are parameters of the readout gate. Finally, the memory attention is calculated by

𝐀mem,t(l)\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{\text{mem},t}^{(l)} =MemoryAttention⁡(𝐇~t,k(l);𝐌t(l))\displaystyle=\operatorname{MemoryAttention}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(l)}_{t,k};\mathbf{M}_{t}^{(l)}\right)
=Concath=1Hq⁡[RMSNorm⁡(𝐑t,h(l))⊙SoftCapSiLU⁡(𝐆t,h(l))],\displaystyle=\operatorname{Concat}_{h=1}^{H_{q}}\left[\operatorname{RMSNorm}\left(\mathbf{R}_{t,h}^{(l)}\right)\odot\operatorname{SoftCapSiLU}\left(\mathbf{G}_{t,h}^{(l)}\right)\right],

where

SoftCapSiLU⁡(x)=τ​tanh⁡(SiLU⁡(x)τ),SiLU⁡(x)=x​σ​(x),\operatorname{SoftCapSiLU}(x)=\tau\tanh\left(\frac{\operatorname{SiLU}(x)}{\tau}\right),\qquad\operatorname{SiLU}(x)=x\,\sigma(x),

and τ>0\tau>0 controls the soft-cap threshold, with τ=2\tau=2 by default. Target layers, projection strategies, and other settings vary slightly to accommodate different backbones, and more details can be found in Appendix B.

2.3 Scaling Native Memory Capacity

To jointly scale the online memory capacity and the trainable memory parameters, we introduce Mixture-of-Storage (MoS), as presented in Figure 5, which expands a native memory block into EE parallel memory experts. Unlike conventional sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) [17], MoS adopts dense routing over all memory experts, so every expert participates in the memory computation and the routing probabilities determine how information is read from and written into different memory experts.

Memory Expert Expansion. For the ll-th MoS layer, we extend the local memory state with an additional expert dimension as

𝓜t,MoS(l)={𝐌t,e(l)}e=1E∈ℝE×Hk​v×dk×dv,\bm{\mathcal{M}}_{t,\mathrm{MoS}}^{(l)}=\left\{\mathbf{M}_{t,e}^{(l)}\right\}_{e=1}^{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times H_{kv}\times d_{k}\times d_{v}},

where 𝐌t,e(l)∈ℝHk​v×dk×dv\mathbf{M}_{t,e}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{kv}\times d_{k}\times d_{v}} is the dynamic memory state of the ee-th expert, and each expert has independent hyper memory parameters. All experts and both routers receive the same pre-attention hidden states 𝐇~t(l)\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t}^{(l)}.

Shared-Address Routing. MoS introduces two dense routers to control memory utilization and memory storage separately, which share a trainable expert address matrix

𝐂(l)=[𝐜1(l),𝐜2(l),⋯,𝐜E(l)]⊤∈ℝE×daddr,\mathbf{C}^{(l)}=\left[\mathbf{c}_{1}^{(l)},\mathbf{c}_{2}^{(l)},\cdots,\mathbf{c}_{E}^{(l)}\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times d_{\mathrm{addr}}},

where daddrd_{\mathrm{addr}} is the dimension of the address representation. Then, we use router projections 𝐖route/u(l),𝐖route/s(l)∈ℝd×daddr\mathbf{W}_{\text{route/u}}^{(l)},\mathbf{W}_{\text{route/s}}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{addr}}} for memory utilization and storage separately. After that, routing probabilities of memory utilization are calculated by

𝜶u,t(l)=Softmax⁡(𝐇~t(l)​𝐖route/u(l)​𝐂(l)⊤)∈ℝLt×E.\bm{\alpha}_{\text{u},t}^{(l)}=\Softmax\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t}^{(l)}\mathbf{W}_{\text{route/u}}^{(l)}\mathbf{C}^{(l)\top}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{t}\times E}.

Similarly, routing probabilities of memory storage are obtained by

𝜶s,t(l)=Softmax⁡(𝐇~t(l)​𝐖route/s(l)​𝐂(l)⊤)∈ℝLt×E.\bm{\alpha}_{\text{s},t}^{(l)}=\Softmax\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t}^{(l)}\mathbf{W}_{\text{route/s}}^{(l)}\mathbf{C}^{(l)\top}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{t}\times E}.

Both softmax operations are applied along the expert dimension. Therefore, the utilization and storage routers share the same semantic expert addresses but learn different projections.

Mixture-of-Storage Fusion. For memory utilization, each expert independently follows the native memory utilization procedure described above. We denote the memory-attention output of the ee-th memory expert by

𝐀mem,t,e(l)=MemoryAttentione⁡(𝐇~t(l);𝐌t,e(l)).\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{mem},t,e}^{(l)}=\operatorname{MemoryAttention}_{e}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t}^{(l)};\mathbf{M}_{t,e}^{(l)}\right).

The final memory attention at the ii-th token in sequence StS_{t} is obtained by

𝐀mem,t,i(l)=∑e=1E𝜶u,t,i,e(l)​𝐀mem,t,i,e(l).\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{mem},t,i}^{(l)}=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\bm{\alpha}_{\text{u},t,i,e}^{(l)}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{mem},t,i,e}^{(l)}.

For memory storage, each expert independently produces its memory key, value, erase gate, write gate, and log-decay using its expert-specific parameters. For the ee-th expert, the erase gate, write gate, and log-decay are calculated by

𝜷~t,e(l)=𝜶s,t,e(l)⊙𝜷t,e(l),𝝎~t,e(l)=𝜶s,t,e(l)⊙𝝎t,e(l),𝝀~t,e(l)=𝝀t,e(l).\tilde{\bm{\beta}}_{t,e}^{(l)}=\bm{\alpha}_{\text{s},t,e}^{(l)}\odot\bm{\beta}_{t,e}^{(l)},\qquad\tilde{\bm{\omega}}_{t,e}^{(l)}=\bm{\alpha}_{\text{s},t,e}^{(l)}\odot\bm{\omega}_{t,e}^{(l)},\qquad\tilde{\bm{\lambda}}_{t,e}^{(l)}=\bm{\lambda}_{t,e}^{(l)}.

After that, we calculate

𝐔t,e(l)=𝜷~t,e(l)⊙𝐊t,e(l).\mathbf{U}_{t,e}^{(l)}=\sqrt{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}_{t,e}^{(l)}}\odot\mathbf{K}_{t,e}^{(l)}.

Finally, the memory state can be updated by

𝐌~t,i,e,h(l)=[𝐈−𝐔t,i,e,h(l)⊤​𝐔t,i,e,h(l)]⋅𝐃~t,i,e,h(l)​𝐌~t,i−1,e,h(l)+𝐔t,i,e,h(l)⊤​(𝝎~t,i,e,h(l)⊙𝐕t,i,e,h(l)),\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}=\left[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{U}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)\top}\mathbf{U}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}\right]\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,i-1,e,h}^{(l)}+\mathbf{U}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)\top}\left(\tilde{\bm{\omega}}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}\odot\mathbf{V}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}\right),

where we have the initialization 𝐌~t,0,e,h(l)=𝐌t,e,h(l)\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,0,e,h}^{(l)}=\mathbf{M}_{t,e,h}^{(l)}, and transformation 𝐌t+1,e,h(l)=𝐌~t,Lt,e,h(l)\mathbf{M}_{t+1,e,h}^{(l)}=\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,L_{t},e,h}^{(l)}, with

𝐃~t,i,e,h(l)=Diag⁡[exp⁡(𝝀~t,i,e,h(l))].\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}=\operatorname{Diag}\left[\exp\left(\tilde{\bm{\lambda}}_{t,i,e,h}^{(l)}\right)\right].

3 Training

3.1 Backbone Preparation

A memory foundation model inherits from its backbone both the knowledge fixed at pre-training and the reliability with which that knowledge becomes behavior, and post-training treats the two very differently. Training on the backbone’s own verified samples fits its distribution conditioned on verifier acceptance [18, 19]: it reweights what the backbone already produces and, by itself, leaves tasks the backbone almost never solves untouched. Our per-item analysis bears this out. Gains concentrate on tasks the backbone solves occasionally. Tasks it never solved in eight attempts end at only 1.6–4.0% accuracy across four benchmarks after the preparation described below, in line with observations for RL [20], whereas on a separate probe set of hard knowledge questions, supplying the relevant facts in context raises accuracy from 27% to 91%, which suggests that the remaining gap is largely informational. In our setting, reliability is therefore what post-training mainly improves, and new information is what native memory must supply.

Accordingly, we post-train DeepSeek-V4-Flash before attaching native memory, with data from a three-step pipeline applied within each of three tracks: general capabilities (instruction following, knowledge, mathematics, and long-context reasoning), agentic coding, and agentic working (tool use and workflow automation). First, capability profiling: each task is attempted repeatedly and classified as reliably, occasionally, or not solved, a profile that stands in for the pre-training data we cannot see. Second, attribution by intervention: a failure is re-run with the suspected missing piece, a grader convention, a procedural hint, or a fact, placed in context, and whether it disappears tells a missing convention or procedure apart from missing knowledge; failures that persist under every intervention are excluded from synthesis. Third, capability-conditioned synthesis assigns each class its own data source. Reliably solved tasks supply replay. Occasionally solved tasks supply the backbone’s own attempts that pass programmatic verifiers (constraint checkers, unit tests, or sandboxed agent runs), which keeps most of the data on the backbone’s own distribution. Failures traced to a missing convention or procedure are learned either from guided sampling, where the guidance appears in the sampling context but not in the target, or from style-matched demonstrations by stronger models. Knowledge gaps, which synthesis has so far closed only item by item, are left mainly to retrieval and, in MemT-1.0, to native memory. Transfer is checked on held-out task families.

The recipe was settled over five rounds of full-mixture training and more than fifty training runs in total. The final mixture holds 126.5K trajectories (2.4B tokens, 1.1B loss-bearing), 56.4% general, 18.0% agentic coding, and 25.3% agentic working by count; agentic trajectories account for about 90% of loss-bearing tokens, so general data anchors the backbone’s existing capabilities while the long agentic trajectories carry the multi-turn behavior that memory tasks build on. The prepared backbone improves on all six benchmarks we monitor across the three tracks, by 6.3 points on average over the public release (Figure 2), and on SWE-bench Multilingual and IFBench v2, at 284B total and 13B active parameters, it exceeds the reported scores of larger open models, including GLM-5.3 Flash (320B total, 18B active) [21] and the far larger DeepSeek-V4 Pro (1.6T total, 49B active) [16].

The backbone is then frozen to serve as both the host model and the full-context distillation teacher of Section 3.3. Backbone preparation and native memory are two routes by which experience shapes a model’s later behavior, through the weights before deployment and through memory states during interaction; closing the loop between them is left to future work.

3.2 Data Construction

To support the training of MemT-1.0, we construct a large-scale training corpus with 34B tokens, which is composed of continued pre-training (CPT) and post-training data. We collect 20B tokens of CPT data, which mainly consists of large-scale general-purpose language modeling corpora. It contains long-form and sequential text to expose the model to diverse linguistic patterns and extensive contextual dependencies.

For post-training, we organize 14B tokens of data into three major categories. First, we construct memory-native language modeling data. This data encourages MemT-1.0 to maintain linguistic coherence, stylistic consistency, and instruction-following capability when information is accessed through native memory. Second, we construct data for native memory storage and utilization, including tasks such as summarization, continuation, and compression. They provide explicit supervision for storing information that should be retained in native memory. They train the model to recover and utilize the stored information during subsequent generation. Third, we introduce memory task data to further strengthen the model’s long-range memory capability. They further improve the model’s ability to selectively retain critical information and resolve long-range dependencies, which improves the utilization of memory when answering downstream queries. Part of the training corpus is based on real-world interaction patterns in MemOS’s anonymized internal data.

All three categories are formulated in a unified context-query-answer format. The context is first processed and stored through the native memory mechanism, after which the model receives the corresponding query and is trained to generate the target answer conditioned on the resulting memory state. This unified formulation allows heterogeneous memory-related tasks to be incorporated into the same post-training pipeline.

3.3 Training Objectives

The core training objective of MemT-1.0 is to align its capability with the backbone given full context, which enables the model to retain and utilize historical information without preserving the context. To this end, we introduce an off-policy distillation framework for training native memory models, where the backbone serves as the teacher model for acquiring memory capabilities [22].

Let θb\theta_{b} denote the frozen backbone parameters and ϕ\phi denote the trainable memory parameters, including the hyper memory blocks and extra parameters of MoS. For a training trajectory {(Xt,Yt)}t=1T\{(X_{t},Y_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}, we define the preceding textual history as C<t=S1​‖⋯‖​St−1C_{<t}=S_{1}\|\cdots\|S_{t-1}, where St=Xt|YtS_{t}=X_{t}\|Y_{t}. We use the original backbone without the additional memory modules as the teacher, whose next-token distribution is

qt,k​(v)=P⁡(v∣C<t,Xt,Yt,<k;θb),v∈𝒱.q_{t,k}(v)=P\left(v\mid C_{<t},X_{t},Y_{t,<k};\theta_{b}\right),\qquad v\in\mathcal{V}.

The MemT-1.0 student receives the current input and the same observed response prefix, with previous steps represented by the incoming local memory state 𝐌t\mathbf{M}_{t}, where

pt,k​(v)=P⁡(v∣Xt,Yt,<k;θb,ϕ,𝓜t).p_{t,k}(v)=P\left(v\mid X_{t},Y_{t,<k};\theta_{b},\phi,\bm{\mathcal{M}}_{t}\right).

Here, 𝓜t\bm{\mathcal{M}}_{t} denotes the collection of dynamic states across all memory layers and experts. The state is initialized to zero for each independent trajectory and evolves through the native storage procedure after each completed step. Both models are evaluated under teacher forcing on fixed teacher-generated trajectories rather than student-generated rollouts, making the distillation objective off-policy with respect to the student policy. To reduce the size of the teacher targets, we retain its Top-KK tokens at each supervised position. Let 𝒦t,k⊆𝒱\mathcal{K}_{t,k}\subseteq\mathcal{V} be this token set and Td>0T_{d}>0 be the distillation temperature. Given qTdq^{T_{d}} and pTdp^{T_{d}} for distributions obtained by dividing the respective logits by TdT_{d} before softmax, we define

q^t,k​(v)=qt,kTd​(v)∑u∈𝒦t,kqt,kTd​(u),v∈𝒦t,k,\hat{q}_{t,k}(v)=\frac{q^{T_{d}}_{t,k}(v)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{K}_{t,k}}q^{T_{d}}_{t,k}(u)},\qquad v\in\mathcal{K}_{t,k},

and set q^t,k​(v)=0\hat{q}_{t,k}(v)=0 outside this set. The per-token distillation loss is the forward KL divergence from this truncated teacher distribution to the student by

ℓt,kKL=Td2​∑v∈𝒦t,kq^t,k​(v)​log⁡q^t,k​(v)pt,kTd​(v).\ell^{\mathrm{KL}}_{t,k}=T_{d}^{2}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{K}_{t,k}}\hat{q}_{t,k}(v)\log\frac{\hat{q}_{t,k}(v)}{p^{T_{d}}_{t,k}(v)}.

The teacher is renormalized over its selected support, whereas the student remains normalized over the full vocabulary. Consequently, the loss also penalizes student probability mass assigned outside the teacher’s selected tokens. We additionally use the observed target token yt,ky_{t,k} for next-token cross-entropy supervision

ℓt,kCE=−log⁡pt,k​(yt,k).\ell^{\mathrm{CE}}_{t,k}=-\log p_{t,k}(y_{t,k}).

For a training batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, let mt,k(b)∈{0,1}m^{(b)}_{t,k}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether a position in trajectory bb is supervised. The training loss is

ℒ⁡(ϕ)=1Nspt​∑b∈ℬ∑t,kmt,k(b)​[λKD​ℓt,kKL,(b)+λCE​ℓt,kCE,(b)],\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{spt}}}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{t,k}m^{(b)}_{t,k}\left[\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}}\ell^{\mathrm{KL},(b)}_{t,k}+\lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}\ell^{\mathrm{CE},(b)}_{t,k}\right],

where Nspt=∑b∈ℬ∑t,kmt,k(b)N_{\mathrm{spt}}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{t,k}m^{(b)}_{t,k} is the number of supervised tokens, and λKD\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}} and λCE\lambda_{\mathrm{CE}} are nonnegative weights with at least one nonzero value. Cross-entropy uses the untempered student distribution. The mask selects the prediction targets appropriate to each training stage and excludes padding. History tokens may participate in memory construction without receiving direct loss. Normalization is performed over all supervised tokens in the optimization batch, including those distributed across workers and accumulation steps. Specifically, we use CE supervision during CPT and KL-based distillation during post-training. For MoS training, we add a router auxiliary loss to balance the load across memory experts. For MemT-1.0-Flash, the backbone prepared in Section 3.1 is frozen during native-memory training.

3.4 Continued Pre-Training

We first conduct CPT to establish the basic capability of language modeling with native memory. This stage trains MemT-1.0 to predict subsequent tokens using both the current textual context and information accumulated from preceding segments. For each training sequence, we divide the tokens into consecutive, non-overlapping segments and treat each segment as a step tt. The student performs causal language modeling within the current segment, with the preceding history C<tC_{<t} represented by the incoming memory states 𝓜t\bm{\mathcal{M}}_{t}. Its backbone context is restricted to the current segment, so information from earlier segments is accessed through native memory. After processing a segment, the native storage procedure applies token-level updates to obtain 𝓜t+1\bm{\mathcal{M}}_{t+1} for the next segment. The final segment is retained even when it is shorter than the specified segment length. Memory states are carried across segments within the same sequence and initialized to zero at the beginning of each independent sequence.

We use CE loss during CPT, with the ground-truth next tokens serving as the supervision targets. The student performs causal language modeling within the current segment while relying on native memory to access information from preceding segments. This encourages the model to establish language modeling capabilities under native memory without requiring the full historical context as textual input.

3.5 Post-Training

Post-training further adapts MemT-1.0 to native memory-based response generation. We initialize the memory parameters from the CPT checkpoint and train on instances containing historical context, queries, and reference responses. The historical context is processed chronologically through the native storage procedure, producing the memory states used to answer subsequent queries. The responses are rollouts from the full-context teacher, and serve to condition both models under teacher forcing rather than as direct supervision targets. At step tt, the student receives the current query XtX_{t} and the observed response prefix Yt,<kY_{t,<k}, with the preceding history C<tC_{<t} represented by 𝓜t\bm{\mathcal{M}}_{t}. The teacher retains access to the corresponding textual history. Memory states are initialized independently for each trajectory, preserving the association between a query and its own history.

We use the KL loss in the post-training stage. The supervision mask mt,k(b)m^{(b)}_{t,k} selects response tokens, while history, query, and padding positions receive no direct token loss. Both teacher and student are evaluated under teacher forcing with the same observed response prefix. Reference responses thus determine the prefixes on which the models are evaluated, while the teacher’s probability distributions provide the distillation targets. The loss is averaged over all supervised response tokens in the training batch. This focuses optimization on the outputs required by the task while training the student to approximate the full-context teacher through native memory. Although historical tokens receive no direct loss, gradients from response predictions propagate through memory readout and earlier storage operations. This allows the model to learn which historical information to retain and how to utilize it for the current query. The full-context teacher provides a reference for both the use of historical information and the backbone’s response behavior, encouraging MemT-1.0 to acquire task-specific memory capabilities while preserving its general capabilities.

3.6 Training Setups

For MemT-1.0-Nano, training consists of 1 CPT epoch followed by post-training. The global batch size is 64 packed sequences. Each pack contains at most 64K tokens, while the segment length is 2K tokens. Incomplete final global batches are dropped. For the distillation objective, we retain the teacher’s top-KK tokens at each supervised position with K=64K=64, and set the distillation temperature to Td=1.0T_{d}=1.0. We optimize only the memory parameters using AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, weight decay 0.010.01, and a gradient clipping norm of 1.01.0. We use mixed-precision training. The backbone runs in BF16, while numerically sensitive components (e.g., RMSNorm, Softmax, and memory states) and optimizer states are kept in FP32. A soft cap is applied to the memory output gate, with a limit of 2.0, for training stability. We use a WSD learning rate scheduler for MemT-1.0-Nano training. During CPT, we warm up for 600 steps to a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}, and keep the peak rate constant for the remaining steps. During post-training, we warm up for 500 steps to 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}, keep it constant, and apply cosine decay over the final 1,000 steps to a minimum learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}. For MemT-1.0-Flash, we initialize from the prepared backbone and use a global batch of 192 packs, with the same 64K maximum pack length and 2K-token storage steps. Memory training uses the online backbone teacher with Top-64 targets, temperature 1, and KL loss. The learning-rate schedule has a peak of 8×10−58\times 10^{-5}, a 100-step warmup, and a planned cosine decay over the final steps.

4 System and Infrastructure

Each interaction in MemT-1.0 depends on memory accumulated from earlier steps. Training must combine these dependencies with batched GPU computation, while inference must maintain an independent evolving state for each trajectory. Our infrastructure executes the model one decoder layer at a time, handles state recurrence within memory blocks, and manages model weights separately from trajectory-specific states. We describe the resulting training schedule, memory operators, and online state organization below.

4.1 Distributed Training

Training packs combine independent trajectories, each containing the steps defined in Section 3. Attention stays within each step, while memory carries information between steps of the same trajectory and resets at trajectory boundaries. Teacher forcing supplies all tokens in the pack, so the model processes the complete pack one decoder layer at a time. Within each layer, attention and memory projections are batched across tokens. The memory block alone advances state along each trajectory. This organization retains large backbone matrix multiplications while preserving the order of memory writes and reads.

We use Megatron-Core [23] and Bridge [24] for distributed training, including expert parallelism for the backbone MoE layers. Although backbone weights are frozen during memory training, gradients still pass through backbone computations and memory transitions, allowing later predictions to train earlier writes. The remaining infrastructure challenge is therefore the cost of memory computation and its training activations, which we address below.

4.2 Efficient Operators

Native memory introduces two related costs: ordered state updates and activations that grow with the number of memory experts. Our execution separates state updates from reads of step snapshots, then groups complete steps into windows to limit the lifetime of expert projections. This lets the memory branch control its working set while the backbone continues to process the full token pack layer by layer.

Chunked updates and snapshot reads. The stable update has a rank-one structure. Suppressing layer, step, and channel indices, let 𝐤i\mathbf{k}_{i} denote the normalized key, and define 𝐮i=𝜷i⊙𝐤i\mathbf{u}_{i}=\sqrt{\bm{\beta}_{i}}\odot\mathbf{k}_{i}, 𝐳i=𝝎i⊙𝐯i\mathbf{z}_{i}=\bm{\omega}_{i}\odot\mathbf{v}_{i}, and 𝐃i=Diag⁡(exp⁡(𝝀i))\mathbf{D}_{i}=\operatorname{Diag}(\exp(\bm{\lambda}_{i})). The update in Section 2 can then be written as

𝐒i=𝐃i​𝐒i−1+𝐮i⊤​(𝐳i−𝐮i​𝐃i​𝐒i−1),𝐒0=𝐌t,𝐌t+1=𝐒Lt.\mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathbf{D}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i-1}+\mathbf{u}_{i}^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{D}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i-1}\bigr),\qquad\mathbf{S}_{0}=\mathbf{M}_{t},\quad\mathbf{M}_{t+1}=\mathbf{S}_{L_{t}}.

Each token requires a vector–matrix multiplication and an outer product, with leading work of O⁡(dk​dv)O(d_{k}d_{v}) per channel. We use chunked WY [25] to group these small dependent updates into triangular solves and matrix multiplications, carrying state between chunks and reconstructing intermediate quantities during backward. The adaptation to MemT-1.0 is to pair this writer with a separate snapshot reader: all queries in step tt read the same incoming state 𝐌t\mathbf{M}_{t}, even as the writer processes several chunks to form 𝐌t+1\mathbf{M}_{t+1}. The reads can therefore be batched independently, followed by RMSNorm and SoftCapSiLU output gating. Gradients from later reads propagate through the writes that produced their snapshots. Writer chunks determine computation granularity, and model steps determine when updated memory becomes visible.

Complete-step windows for MoS. Dense MoS evaluates every expert, so materializing all expert projections at once requires tensors that grow with both pack length and expert count. Whole-pack execution does exactly this: it projects every token in the pack before processing the resulting memory computations. Windowed execution instead performs expert projections, state updates, and readout fusion for one group of complete steps at a time, passing a differentiable FP32 final state to the next window. Both schedules use the same storage and utilization routers, shared expert addresses, and update kernel. Storage probabilities modulate the erase gate, write gate, and log-decay. Utilization probabilities mix the gated expert readouts.

A window budget limits how many tokens are projected together, while keeping each step intact even if it exceeds the budget. Recomputing internal intermediates during backward [26] avoids retaining all windows’ expert projections for the full training pass. Smaller windows reduce live intermediates but require more launches and recomputation. Outputs, routing probabilities, and boundary states still occupy memory, so the total remains dependent on pack length as well as window size.

The memory–time tradeoff of window size. We measure one complete MoS memory block on a single GPU using synthetic hidden-state inputs. Table 1 fixes a 32K-token pack, BF16 parameters and projections, and 2048-token steps, comparing peak allocated memory and forward-plus-backward (F+B) time for two window sizes. Arrows denote whole-pack execution →\rightarrow windowed execution; all values are medians.

In this configuration, processing two steps at a time reduces peak memory by approximately 80%, with a 1.6% increase in median F+B time. Shrinking the window to one step saves additional memory but raises the time increase to 6.6%. The window budget thus provides a direct resource tradeoff: smaller windows reduce live intermediates, while larger windows reduce execution overhead. Appendix F provides the block configuration, measurement protocol, and full results and variability from 8K to 32K.

4.3 Stateful Inference and Serving

During online interaction, backbone and hyper memory weights remain fixed and are shared across trajectories, while each trajectory maintains its own dynamic memory states. Within a step, generation reads the incoming memory snapshot, and attention over the current text uses that step’s KV cache. Once the interaction completes, storage incorporates the input and response into memory for the next interaction. The serving runtime manages states by trajectory so that subsequent requests continue their respective histories.

For a fixed configuration, the number of memory-state elements per trajectory is

Nstate=∑lEl​Hk​v,l​dk,l​dv,l,N_{\mathrm{state}}=\sum_{l}E_{l}H_{kv,l}d_{k,l}d_{v,l},

where the sum covers memory layers and El=1E_{l}=1 without MoS. Growing history updates these elements while their number remains determined by configured memory capacity. Total storage for multiple trajectories grows with trajectory count. Active requests additionally require their current-step KV caches and computational workspaces. Persistent-state storage can thus be estimated directly from the memory configuration, whereas runtime GPU memory also includes shared weights and active requests. The effect of finite capacity on retained historical detail is examined in the capability evaluations and Discussion.

This organization separates history preparation from subsequent queries. In Evaluation’s two-GPU, single-request BEAM experiment, MemT-1.0-Nano’s query latency after history preparation remains nearly constant as history grows. At 64K tokens of history, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves an approximately 33×\times reduction in logical per-trajectory state size compared with full context. The storage metric measures the logical state size after history preparation and before querying, and excludes shared weights. When subsequent queries reuse that state, the initial preparation cost is amortized over multiple interactions. The full protocol and curves appear in Section 6 and Appendix D.5.

5 Memory Scaling Behavior

5.1 Overview

Scaling has been a key driver behind the continuous improvement of foundation models, where increasing model capacity, training data, and computation often leads to predictable gains in general capabilities [11]. However, for memory foundation models, it remains unclear whether native memory capabilities exhibit similar scaling behavior. Exploring such scaling behavior is critical, as it reveals whether memory capability can continue to improve with scale and provides guidance for the design of larger memory foundation models. In particular, memory-related training and the capacity of native memory states are two important factors that may influence memory capability, motivating us to explore scaling behavior along these two aspects.

In this work, we study memory scaling along both dimensions. Data and training scaling explores how memory capability changes with continued exposure to memory-related post-training data, while memory capacity scaling studies the impact of increasing the capacity of native memory states. They allow us to characterize how native memory capability evolves with additional training and expanded memory capacity.

5.2 Scaling Protocol

We conduct all scaling experiments based on MemT-1.0-Nano under a controlled experimental protocol. We explore two scaling aspects, including data and training scaling and memory capacity scaling. The backbone architecture, training objectives, and evaluation protocol are kept consistent across different configurations unless otherwise specified. We evaluate memory capability using the same memory benchmarks to characterize performance changes across different scales.

Specifically, for data and training scaling, we evaluate checkpoints along a continuous post-training trajectory spanning two consecutive epochs over the same corpus. The model architecture and training corpus remain fixed, while cumulative training exposure and optimization steps increase throughout training. For memory capacity scaling, we vary the number of memory experts in MoS to expand native memory capacity, while keeping the remaining architectural components and training configurations consistent. By examining the resulting performance curves, we investigate how native memory capability evolves with additional post-training and increased memory capacity.

5.3 Data and Training Scaling

We explore whether additional exposure to memory-related post-training data improves memory capability at a fixed model capacity. Starting from the CPT checkpoint, we follow a single MemT-1.0-Nano training trajectory for two epochs over the same post-training corpus.

Figure 6 shows that memory performance generally improves with additional post-training. Across the sampled checkpoints, the average score increases from 36.65 to 46.80, with intermediate fluctuations. Most of this gain arrives early: the average score rises steeply within the first quarter epoch and continues to climb over the remainder of the first epoch, reaching 45.40 by its end, while LoCoMo improves from 40.39 to 55.39 over the same span. This pattern is consistent with rapid adaptation of the CPT-initialized memory modules to downstream query answering, after which the increments shrink steadily but do not disappear. In the second epoch, the final sampled checkpoint reaches 46.80 on average and 57.53 on LoCoMo, an improvement over the last sampled checkpoint of the first epoch despite intermediate fluctuations. These gains indicate remaining room for optimization at fixed memory capacity, even when training revisits previously seen data. In summary, continued exposure to memory-related post-training data can improve native memory capability, with further gains achievable across epochs without increasing model capacity.

5.4 Memory Capacity Scaling

Following 400 steps of CPT, we explore memory capacity scaling during post-training by comparing MoS configurations with 2 and 4 memory experts. We evaluate both of them at 200, 3,400, and 5,500 post-training steps, reporting the average score alongside the LoCoMo score. The results are presented in Figure 7. The 4-expert configuration consistently outperforms the 2-expert configuration across all three checkpoints, with relatively modest gains of 0.41 points in the average score and 1.42 points on LoCoMo at 200 post-training steps. At 3,400 and 5,500 steps, increasing the number of experts improves the average score by 2.01 and 2.69 points, respectively, and LoCoMo by 3.25 and 2.20 points. The 4-expert configuration continues to improve between these later checkpoints, with its average score increasing from 44.29 to 44.68 and its LoCoMo score rising from 53.51 to 55.58. These results suggest that expanding memory capacity through additional experts benefits downstream performance, with larger gains at the later post-training checkpoints than at 200 steps.

6 Evaluation

6.1 Overall Evaluation Setup

We evaluate MemT-1.0 from the perspectives of memory and general capabilities. The memory evaluation focuses on whether MemT-1.0 can answer questions based on its dynamic memory states, without access to prior textual context. The evaluation on general capabilities examines the impact of the additional native memory mechanism on the model’s general capabilities. These aspects provide an important foundation for self-evolving memory-native models.

Benchmarks. We evaluate memory capabilities on 11 benchmarks and divide them into four groups according to trajectory length. Specifically, the group below 16K includes MemBench [27] and ImplicitMemBench [28], and the 16K-32K group includes PersonaMem [29], PS-Bench [30], and LoCoMo [31]. For longer trajectories, the 32K-64K group includes PerMemSafe [32], Memora [33], and MemOps [34], and the group above 64K includes LongMemEval-S [35], MemoryAgentBench [36], and BEAM-1M [37]. These benchmarks focus on long-term information retention and retrieval, dynamic memory updating and management, and personalized understanding. In addition, we evaluate general capabilities on six benchmarks spanning four major dimensions. Specifically, we evaluate knowledge and scientific reasoning with MMLU-Pro [38] and GPQA Diamond [39], instruction following with IFEval [40], long-context understanding with LongBench v2 [41], and code generation with BigCodeBench-Hard [42] and LiveCodeBench v6 [43]. These benchmarks collectively assess a wide range of general capabilities, thereby reflecting the impact of the additional native memory mechanism on the underlying backbone model. More details are available in Appendix D.1.

Baselines. We compare MemT-1.0 with textual memory and parametric memory approaches. Textual memory methods perform inference based on the original backbone model with full context and partial context settings. Full context provides the complete historical text as memory in the input context, while DenseRAG retrieves a subset of relevant information as contextual evidence [44]. We also include representative memory systems for comparison, including MemOS [45], Mem0 [46], OpenViking [47], and Graphiti [48]. For parametric memory methods, no textual history is provided in the context, and the model performs inference using its own parametric memory. Our parametric memory baselines include Temp-LoRA [49], Doc-to-LoRA [50], SHINE [51], δ\delta-mem [52], LiveMem [53], MemoryLLM [54] and ICAE [55]. More details of the baselines are provided in Appendix D.2.

Evaluation Protocol. For memory capability evaluation, in each trajectory, we first reset the memory and write the historical information into memory following the chronological order. Then, the model is required to answer multiple questions related to the historical information, and the responses are compared against the ground-truth answers to compute accuracy. Specifically, memory is strictly isolated across different users and histories. Ground-truth answers, evidence annotations, and evaluation labels are only used for scoring and are never exposed to the evaluated models. For LLM-as-a-Judge, we utilize gpt-4.1-mini with the OmniMemEval [56] prompt. For general capability evaluation, we introduce irrelevant information before inference, which aims to examine how the native memory mechanism affects the model’s general capabilities under the noise setting. More details are available in Appendix D.4.

6.2 Memory Capabilities

The results for memory capabilities are presented in Table 2. MemT-1.0-Flash and MemT-1.0-Nano achieve average scores of 50.6 and 47.0, respectively, ranking first and second among the parametric memory methods, ahead of the strongest parametric baseline by 12.5 and 8.9 points. The results support native memory as a shared representation for diverse memory tasks without providing historical text in the query context. The comparison between MemT-1.0-Flash and MemT-1.0-Nano reveals distinct strengths across tasks, though the aggregate gap between them remains modest and is driven mainly by memory operations. MemT-1.0-Flash improves most clearly on memory operations, personalized understanding, conversational recall, and implicit learning. MemT-1.0-Nano remains stronger on PerMemSafe and Memora, whereas MemT-1.0-Flash scores higher on Persona-grounded PS-Bench. The advantage over parametric memory baselines also extends to long histories, where MemT-1.0 leads this group on LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench, and BEAM-1M. However, the remaining errors on these benchmarks show that processing an extended trajectory does not by itself ensure reliable access to its contents. Answering later queries requires earlier information to survive successive updates and remain distinguishable from other stored associations. The results motivate further improvements in selective retention and query-dependent readout.

The strongest textual memory systems still achieve substantially higher performance, particularly on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-1M. These systems provide explicit historical evidence at query time, whereas MemT-1.0 must recover the required information from its evolving states. This gap is consistent with the difficulty of preserving detailed evidence through recurrent memory updates and highlights memory fidelity as an important target for further development.

6.3 General Capabilities

We evaluate general capabilities under the noise setting. In this setting, we inject irrelevant information into memory before the evaluation tasks, which simulates the impact of distracting memories during real-world online interactions. We report the performance gap between MemT-1.0 and its corresponding backbone model under the noise setting. The results are presented in Table 3.

MemT-1.0-Flash performs comparably to its DeepSeek-V4-Flash backbone on average under the same noise setting. The largest gain occurs on BigCodeBench-Hard, with smaller improvements on IFEval and LongBench v2. Performance decreases modestly on MMLU-Pro, GPQA Diamond, and LiveCodeBench v6. These results suggest that MemT-1.0-Flash broadly preserves general capabilities under distracting memories.

We next examine MemT-1.0-Nano, whose average decrease is around one point. Under the noise setting, most benchmarks remain close to the backbone, with gains on IFEval and BigCodeBench-Hard. The degradation is concentrated rather than uniform. The largest decrease occurs on LiveCodeBench v6, followed by smaller decreases on LongBench v2, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA Diamond. The contrasting changes on BigCodeBench-Hard and LiveCodeBench v6 further suggest that the impact varies even across benchmarks within the same capability domain.

Overall, the results support broad capability preservation alongside native memory, while highlighting that resistance to distracting memories should be evaluated at the task level.

6.4 Ablation Studies

In this section, we further present several ablation studies based on MemT-1.0-Nano during model development. As for the model architecture, we focus on the update rule and update granularity in the native memory procedure. We also design a bidirectional encoding mechanism to aggregate information from the current turn. In addition, we study the contribution of different training stages. These experiments further verify the effectiveness of our current architecture.

6.4.1 Architecture Ablation

For architecture ablation, we evaluate four variants. First, we remove the stable mechanism to recover the GDN-2 memory update (w/ GDN-2) by directly using

𝐌~t,i,h(l)=[𝐈−𝐊t,i,h(l)⊤​(𝜷t,i,h(l)⊙𝐊t,i,h(l))]⋅𝐃t,i,h(l)​𝐌~t,i−1,h(l)+𝐊t,i,h(l)⊤​(𝝎t,i,h(l)⊙𝐕t,i,h(l)).\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}=\left[\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{K}_{t,i,h}^{(l)\top}\left(\bm{\beta}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\odot\mathbf{K}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\right)\right]\cdot\mathbf{D}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_{t,i-1,h}^{(l)}+\mathbf{K}_{t,i,h}^{(l)\top}\left(\bm{\omega}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\odot\mathbf{V}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\right).

We also change the update rule into GDN [57] as another ablation baseline (w/ GDN). Second, we change the update granularity from token-level to turn-level (w/ TL). The storage procedure can be defined as

𝐌t+1,h(l)=[𝐈−1Lt​𝐔t,h(l)⊤​𝐔t,h(l)]⋅𝐃t,h(l)​𝐌t,h(l)+1Lt​𝐔t,h(l)⊤​(𝝎t,h(l)⊙𝐕t,h(l)),\mathbf{M}_{t+1,h}^{(l)}=\left[\mathbf{I}-\frac{1}{L_{t}}\mathbf{U}_{t,h}^{(l)\top}\mathbf{U}_{t,h}^{(l)}\right]\cdot\mathbf{D}_{t,h}^{(l)}\mathbf{M}_{t,h}^{(l)}+\frac{1}{L_{t}}\mathbf{U}_{t,h}^{(l)\top}\left(\bm{\omega}_{t,h}^{(l)}\odot\mathbf{V}_{t,h}^{(l)}\right),

where we have

𝐃t,h(l)=Diag⁡[exp⁡(1Lt​∑i=1Lt𝝀t,i,h(l))].\mathbf{D}_{t,h}^{(l)}=\operatorname{Diag}\left[\exp\left(\frac{1}{L_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{L_{t}}\bm{\lambda}_{t,i,h}^{(l)}\right)\right].

We also evaluate a bidirectional encoding (w/ BE) for information aggregation. Specifically, during the storage procedure in each turn, it first projects the pre-attention hidden states 𝐇~t(l)\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t}^{(l)} into a lower-dimensional space, and applies multi-head self-attention with rotary position embeddings without a causal mask. After that, it projects the result back to the backbone dimension through a residual connection. The enriched representations are used to predict the erase, write, and forget gates, while the memory keys and values are still projected from the original pre-attention hidden states.

As shown in Table 4, the update granularity has the largest effect among the architecture variants. Replacing token-level with turn-level aggregation reduces the average from 46.97 to 40.98, a far larger drop than any change to the update rule. This may be because successive token-level updates can better account for memory decay and revise associations established earlier within the same turn. The update-rule variants, by contrast, stay close to the full model, with removing the stable mechanism giving 46.43 and substituting GDN giving 46.72. Both fall within a narrow band around the baseline, so the aggregate capability is not determined by the precise form of the update rule. Adding bidirectional encoding reduces the average to 45.43. Its effect is benchmark-dependent rather than uniformly negative: MB, IM, PM, and PMS improve, whereas the remaining benchmarks regress. Under the evaluated training budget, bidirectional encoding does not improve aggregate memory performance, and its benchmark-specific gains do not offset the losses elsewhere.

6.4.2 Training Ablation

We further conduct ablation studies on our training procedures. For the w/o CPT setting, we skip CPT and directly train the memory parameters through post-training alone. For the w/o PT setting, we evaluate the checkpoint after continued pre-training without subsequent post-training. From the results in Table 4, we find that post-training plays an important role in memory-specific tasks, where it increases the average score by approximately 10.69 points over the CPT checkpoint. These results indicate that language-modeling CPT alone does not provide the same memory-conditioned response capability as the complete pipeline. In addition, the CPT stage improves post-training as well. Therefore, post-training accounts for the larger observed gain in this comparison, while CPT provides an additional aggregate benefit as an initialization stage.

6.5 End-to-End Inference Efficiency

We further evaluate the end-to-end inference efficiency of MemT-1.0 against baseline methods, with a particular focus on the results as the history length increases. Specifically, we compare MemT-1.0-Nano with full context, δ\delta-mem, and Temp-LoRA on BEAM. Full context, Temp-LoRA and MemT-1.0-Nano use HF inference on two GPUs exclusively allocated to each run, with backbone layers distributed across devices, a concurrency of 1, and a batch size of 1. For δ\delta-mem, we use its publicly released model and implementation.

We construct input sequences with varying history lengths based on BEAM. The query uses shared 512-token content, with the chat template added separately, rather than a benchmark question, and each sequence is treated independently. We evaluate a fixed generation length of 128 tokens by forcing the model to decode exactly 128 tokens while ignoring the end-of-sequence signal. For the HF evaluations, synchronized wall-clock timers exclude model loading, input tokenization, and evaluation-related scoring overhead. For each history and length, we measure preparation once, discard one query warm-up, and average five timed queries. Reported curves average the resulting values across 35 histories. For MemT-1.0-Nano, history content is processed in 2,048-token slices, with each chat-formatted chunk capped at 2,048 tokens.

The reported end-to-end latency includes history preparation and response generation, accounting for indexing, test-time adaptation, or memory writes as applicable. We additionally report query time to first token (TTFT), measured from the start of query execution to the first generated token, including query prefilling but excluding history preparation. For full context and MemT-1.0-Nano, both end-to-end latency and TTFT include state restoration. The HF full-context baseline reuses the prepared history cache. We report results over the common history-length range from 512 to 256K tokens. Figure 8 presents the results. MemT-1.0-Nano achieves an end-to-end advantage over full context at long histories. It is generally slower at short histories and approximately matches full context at 32K tokens, reaching speedups of approximately 1.20×1.20\times at 64K, 1.86×1.86\times at 128K, and 3.99×3.99\times at 256K. Its memory storage procedure processes history incrementally; generation then accesses the resulting state without retaining historical tokens in the attention context. In comparison, the full-context baseline incurs both history prefilling and continued attention over historical KV entries during generation. The measured long-history end-to-end advantage primarily reflects lower history-preparation cost.

The query TTFT curves reveal an additional benefit after history preparation. MemT-1.0-Nano maintains broadly stable mean query TTFT of approximately 104–112 ms across the evaluated range, while full-context TTFT rises to approximately 257 ms at 128K tokens and 445 ms at 256K tokens. MemT-1.0-Nano’s behavior is consistent with a fixed-size memory readout whose state dimensions do not grow with the number of historical tokens processed. For persistent interactions, it allows accumulated history to influence responses without progressively increasing the attention context used for each new query. The benefit concerns access to the stored representation, and the memory-capability results above already show that this representation preserves useful information. At 128K and 256K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves query TTFT speedups of approximately 2.44×2.44\times and 4.19×4.19\times, respectively, over cached full-context inference.

Previously collected results for the parametric memory baselines highlight the importance of accounting for preparation costs. Temp-LoRA maintains stable query TTFT, but its end-to-end cost grows substantially because history-specific adaptation requires optimization. Although δ\delta-mem has the lowest query TTFT, its end-to-end latency exceeds Nano’s from 64K tokens onward as history-preparation cost grows. Absolute latency differences across these systems also reflect their backbone, runtime, and tokenization configurations. These results show the value of efficient memory construction together with predictable query TTFT. Reusing a prepared state amortizes its construction cost over multiple queries.

6.6 Storage Overhead

We evaluate the per-trajectory storage overhead on BEAM histories, after history preparation and before querying. The reported storage size is the logical size in bytes of the per-trajectory state. The shared backbone weights, embedders and hyper memory parameters are excluded from the measurement. More details can be found in Appendix D.5, and the results are presented in Figure 9.

Figure 9 shows a clear difference between retaining historical records and maintaining a fixed-size state. Full context incurs increasing storage as its logical state size grows with the visible history. DenseRAG has a much smaller storage overhead at short histories, but its stored texts and retrieval vectors also accumulate as more information is added. In contrast, MemT-1.0-Nano’s memory state storage remains constant throughout the trajectory, because new information updates memory states without enlarging them. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves an approximately 66×66\times reduction in per-trajectory storage compared with the full context setting. Temp-LoRA also exhibits constant storage, since its adapter dimensions are fixed, although its storage overhead is larger than MemT-1.0-Nano’s in the evaluated configuration.

The comparison with DenseRAG illustrates how the storage advantage depends on interaction length. For short histories, storing a small collection of text chunks and embeddings is cheaper than allocating MemT-1.0-Nano’s full memory state. As histories grow, DenseRAG’s accumulated records eventually exceed that fixed allocation. MemT-1.0-Nano therefore becomes more attractive for persistent sessions with extended interaction histories, where additional turns do not increase the size of the saved state. The full context curve ends at its context-window limit, so its reported storage does not represent retaining the entire longest history. For deployment of MemT-1.0, a constant state size makes per-trajectory logical-state budgets predictable, and bounds the logical payload that must be saved or transferred when resuming an interaction. Total storage still grows with the number of independent trajectories and the configured memory capacity.

6.7 Low-Rank Decomposition

To further explore the compressibility of memory states based on MemT-1.0-Nano, we perform online low-rank projection for memory states to study their performance impacts. Specifically, we apply singular value decomposition (SVD) to the FP32 state matrix of each layer after each storage procedure, and reconstruct a dense state from the retained components for subsequent computation. For a retained rank kk, the reconstructed state is computed as

𝐌t,h(l)=U:,1:kΣ1:k,1:kV:,1:k⊤.\mathbf{M}_{t,h}^{(l)}=U_{:,1:k}\Sigma_{1:k,1:k}V_{:,1:k}^{\top}.

We set the rank k∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256}k\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256\}, with the full rank k=256k=256 retaining the original dense state without projection. The evaluation is conducted on PersonaMem and LoCoMo. For each retention ratio, we independently initialize the memory state, write the complete history, and apply low-rank reconstruction after every memory storage when k<256k<256.

Figure 10 shows different results across the two tasks. On LoCoMo, accuracy generally improves as more singular components are retained. The largest gains fall in the middle of the rank range, and the final doublings add progressively less, although the score still improves up to the full rank. The one exception is the smallest retained rank, which scores slightly above the next one. At this level of truncation, the small score difference alone does not establish an advantage of extreme compression. PersonaMem follows the same shape but saturates much earlier. Its accuracy rises quickly and then flattens out before reaching full rank, with the highest observed accuracy at an intermediate rank and no further improvement once additional components are retained. Overall, memory performance improves as the retained rank increases, but the returns diminish quickly, and on PersonaMem they eventually vanish. Because theoretical factor storage grows roughly linearly with the retained rank, increasing the rank yields diminishing returns in downstream accuracy.

7 Application in Agentic Tasks

7.1 Overview

In this section, we investigate the potential of MemT-1.0 for developing self-evolving agents through continual learning. We apply MemT-1.0 to long-horizon agentic tasks, where agents must use environment feedback to guide task execution. Real-world agent interactions generate a wealth of trajectories containing valuable procedural experience. Reusing this experience offers a promising path toward improving agent performance across tasks. Current methods typically extract experience from historical trajectories and include it in the textual context of subsequent tasks [58], increasing the burden on an already growing execution context. MemT-1.0 can instead store experience in native memory and use it to guide actions in long-horizon tasks.

We focus on agentic coding and train MemT-1.0-Nano to apply procedural experience extracted from historical trajectories. We evaluate it on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, both without experience and with textual experience. With experience stored before execution, MemT-1.0-Nano improves the proportion of tasks solved in all three runs over the backbone without experience by 7.6 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified and 8.3 points on SWE-bench Multilingual. Results show that MemT-1.0 can improve agentic task performance beyond memory-focused evaluations and support its potential as a foundation for self-evolving agents.

7.2 Experience-Guided Agentic Framework

To explore this potential, we develop an agentic framework in which MemT-1.0 stores and reuses procedural experience during long-horizon task execution. We construct an experience bank by summarizing historical agent trajectories into reusable procedural guidance. As illustrated in Figure 11, the framework retrieves relevant experience from the bank and stores it in either the agent’s textual context or MemT-1.0-Nano’s native memory. The two approaches use the same experience but differ in how it is accessed during task execution.

Experience Retrieval and Storage. Given a coding task, we retrieve relevant experiences from the experience bank using BGE-M3 [59]. Each experience describes its applicable conditions, recommended procedures, and verification strategies. The task description serves as the retrieval query, and candidate experiences are ranked according to embedding similarity. The selected experience is converted into a structured textual representation before storage.

We consider two experience storage settings. In the Before Execution setting, experience is stored before the agent begins execution. In the Harness-Triggered setting, the agent first executes the task independently, and experience is stored when the execution harness detects a critical breakpoint. Such breakpoints are identified using execution feedback, including command failures, empty observations, and repeated unsuccessful operations. The detection only relies on information available during execution, without accessing reference solutions. Each trajectory receives at most one experience store operation.

Memory-Based Experience Application. In the Textual Experience setting, the retrieved experience is directly inserted into the agent’s message history and remains available through the subsequent context. In the Native Memory setting, MemT-1.0-Nano writes the same experience into its native memory state through a separate memory store operation. Specifically, the experience text is processed by a forward pass with memory writing enabled, updating the memory state MM without modifying the original task context. After the memory store operation, agent actions access the stored experience through memory attention, allowing the experience to influence action generation without explicitly appearing in the message history.

Each execution trajectory maintains an independent memory state. The state is initialized to empty before the task and updated when experience is stored. After storing experience, it remains fixed and is read during subsequent execution until it is reset at the end of the trajectory. This setup evaluates whether a trained native-memory agent can effectively reuse procedural experience without retaining the experience text in the task context.

7.3 Experience Construction and Model Training

To enable experience-guided agentic execution through native memory, we construct training data that associate reusable procedural experience with successful execution behaviors. The overall data construction consists of two stages, extracting reusable experience from historical trajectories and generating experience-conditioned trajectories.

Experience Data Construction. We first construct an experience bank from 41,057 successful coding trajectories released by Scale-SWE [60]. Following the experience summarization framework of MSCE [61], the construction process consists of trajectory annotation, procedural policy induction, policy clustering, and experience generation with quality auditing. For each successful trajectory, we identify important execution decisions and their corresponding environmental conditions. Trajectories with similar conditions are grouped to induce reusable procedural policies, which are subsequently consolidated and converted into structured experiences. Each experience contains information about its triggering conditions, recommended execution steps, applicability constraints, and verification procedures. After quality filtering, we obtain an experience bank containing 1,040 reusable coding experiences.

Training Sample Construction. We further construct experience-guided training trajectories through counterfactual execution. Specifically, we generate original coding trajectories using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with the AweAgent harness [62] in the Scale-SWE environment. For unsuccessful trajectories, we identify candidate breakpoints according to execution errors and other observable failure signals. At each selected breakpoint, we retrieve candidate experiences and resume execution with different experience combinations. The resulting trajectories are evaluated using executable tests, and we retain experience-conditioned continuations that pass the task tests when the corresponding original trajectory failed.

Each training sample is represented as

xb,j=(ξ≤b,gb,j,ξ^>b+),x_{b,j}=\left(\xi_{\leq b},g_{b,j},\hat{\xi}_{>b}^{+}\right),

where bb indexes the selected breakpoint and jj indexes the candidate experience subset. Here, ξ≤b\xi_{\leq b} denotes the original trajectory prefix before and including breakpoint bb, gb,jg_{b,j} denotes the injected experience subset, and ξ^>b+\hat{\xi}_{>b}^{+} denotes the successful continuation after experience injection.

The retained samples satisfy the condition that the original trajectory fails while the experience-conditioned continuation succeeds. These continuations provide supervision for predicting successful actions conditioned on procedural experience. We generate 18,820 original trajectories and evaluate 199,500 breakpoint-experience intervention variants. Among these interventions, 45,481 produce successful continuations. After additional quality filtering, we obtain 42,403 training samples. The resulting samples are partitioned by task to avoid leakage between training and validation trajectories. Appendix E provides details of the experience bank, data construction pipeline, and filtering procedure.

Training Strategy. We initialize the model from MemT-1.0-Nano. During application-specific post-training, all backbone parameters are frozen, and only the native hyper memory blocks are optimized. Each training sample is processed through separate experience and main-trajectory streams. First, the experience is written into native memory through a memory store operation. The original trajectory prefix is then replayed with memory reading disabled. After the designated breakpoint, memory reading is enabled, and the model is trained to predict the successful continuation conditioned on the stored experience. The experience text and trajectory prefix are excluded from the training loss, while the subsequent assistant actions provide the supervision signal.

We investigate both cross-entropy supervision and knowledge distillation. For knowledge distillation, the frozen backbone teacher receives the experience as text, while the student accesses the same experience only through native memory. Both models use teacher forcing on the same task history and reference continuation. We minimize the forward KL divergence from the teacher distribution to the student distribution over supervised assistant tokens.

We additionally investigate two supervision scopes. The First-Step setting supervises only the first assistant turn following the breakpoint, and the Full-Suffix setting supervises the complete successful continuation.
