We use knowledge distillation with Full-Suffix supervision for the application-specific post-training of MemT-1.0-Nano and evaluate the resulting checkpoint in the main experiments. Appendix E details the sample serialization and supervision masks.

7.4 Agentic Coding Evaluation

We evaluate MemT-1.0-Nano on two agentic coding benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified [12], containing 500 tasks, and SWE-bench Multilingual [13], containing 300 tasks across nine programming languages. Both benchmarks require agents to resolve real-world software issues through repository exploration, code modifications, and executable tests. All baselines use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone and follow the official SWE-bench verification protocol.

We compare Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (No Experience), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Textual Experience), and MemT-1.0-Nano (Native Memory). The No Experience baseline measures the benefit of experience reuse, while Textual Experience provides a reference for evaluating its effectiveness through native memory. The Harness-Triggered setting uses the same breakpoint-detection logic as training data construction. The Before Execution setting is used to assess robustness to experience injection timing. Each task is executed three times independently.

As shown in Table 5, we report the average success rate, pass@3, representing the proportion of tasks solved at least once across the three runs, and pass^3, representing the proportion of tasks solved in all three runs. MemT-1.0-Nano consistently improves the average success rate and repeated-run reliability over the backbone without experience. On SWE-bench Verified, in the Before Execution setting, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves an average success rate of 69.33%, improving upon the No Experience baseline of 66.07%. This slightly exceeds the 68.87% achieved by Textual Experience. Moreover, pass^3 increases from 54.00% to 61.60%, matching the 61.60% achieved by Textual Experience. These results indicate that native memory can preserve the effectiveness of procedural experience without requiring the corresponding experience text to remain in the task context.

In the Harness-Triggered setting, MemT-1.0-Nano further improves the average success rate to 69.73%, compared with 66.07% for No Experience and 69.13% for rank-1 textual experience. The corresponding pass^3 reaches 62.80%, representing an improvement of 8.80 percentage points over the backbone and 1.00 percentage point over fixed rank-1 textual experience. This suggests that native memory remains effective when experience is introduced dynamically during agent execution, rather than only at task initialization.

We observe consistent improvements on SWE-bench Multilingual. In the Before Execution setting, MemT-1.0-Nano improves the average success rate from 60.00% to 62.89% and pass^3 from 45.33% to 53.67%. In the Harness-Triggered setting, the average success rate reaches 63.56%, exceeding the fixed rank-1 textual experience result of 63.00%. These findings provide further evidence that experience internalization generalizes across coding tasks involving different repositories and programming languages.

The gains are most pronounced in repeated-run reliability, suggesting that stored experience helps agents solve tasks more consistently. Although pass^3 improves substantially, pass@3 does not consistently increase. The comparable behavior of MemT-1.0-Nano and textual experience further suggests that procedural guidance can be represented and utilized through native memory.

We also evaluate several training configurations on a 100-task development subset of SWE-bench Verified. Detailed comparisons and additional experimental results are provided in Appendix E.

7.5 Case Study and Discussion

To better understand how native memory affects agent behavior, we illustrate a representative task from SWE-bench Verified involving the two-digit year parsing logic in Django’s parse_http_date function.

We compare execution trajectories under the No Experience, Textual Experience, and Native Memory settings. Without experience, the agent modifies the relevant parsing logic shortly after locating the implementation, introducing targeted reproduction and verification steps later in the execution. In contrast, agents in both the Textual Experience and Native Memory settings construct reproduction tests before applying modifications. In the MemT-1.0-Nano trajectory, the agent further revisits a boundary condition after its initial modification, corrects the implementation, and performs additional verification.

These observations show how stored procedural experience can guide task execution without appearing in textual context. Together with the benchmark improvements, they demonstrate that MemT-1.0 can reuse procedural experience to improve agentic task performance. This supports its potential for developing self-evolving agents: experience from past interactions can be stored in native memory and applied to new tasks.

Several challenges remain. The current framework relies on externally constructed experience, making its effectiveness dependent on experience quality and retrieval. Storing experience also introduces computation, so reduced textual context does not necessarily imply lower overall execution costs. Extending experience reuse into an autonomous continual learning process remains an open direction.

Future work will explore the co-evolution of the harness and MemT-1.0 through continued interaction with the environment. The harness can improve experience acquisition and selection, while MemT-1.0 learns to reuse that experience more effectively. Together, these advances could support continual learning in self-evolving agents for long-horizon tasks.

8 Limitations and Discussion

Despite the progress of MemT-1.0 in native memory, it still has several limitations. The fixed-size memory state imposes a capacity constraint. For the fixed memory, MemT-1.0 maintains an O⁡(1)O(1) state with respect to the interaction history length NN. Compared with methods whose stored representations grow as O⁡(N)O(N), this bounded state has limited capacity to preserve detailed historical information. As interactions accumulate, new information must be incorporated into an existing representation, creating trade-offs between retaining earlier details and adding recent information. The resulting loss of memory fidelity remains a challenge for tasks requiring precise recall. At the same time, a fixed-size state offers opportunities beyond reducing storage. Each update incorporates new information into a representation, which has already been shaped by earlier interactions. This enables successive compression of accumulated history. Compared with maintaining a growing collection of historical records, this recurrent organization may provide a basis for latent reflection. It potentially allows iterative consolidation of experience within the memory state. Such a mechanism could support online self-evolution by allowing accumulated experience to influence subsequent behavior.

Finally, the relationship between local memory and hyper memory also deserves further study. Local memory represents information accumulated during interaction, while hyper memory encodes learned capabilities for storing and utilizing that information. An important question is whether experience accumulated in local memory can be consolidated into hyper-memory parameters through further training, and how knowledge encoded in hyper memory can be instantiated and adapted through local memory. Therefore, memory capability itself can be viewed as a higher-order form of learned information. Exploring this relationship may help connect adaptation within individual interactions with improvements in memory capability across tasks.

9 Conclusion

In this report, we presented MemT-1.0, a family of memory foundation models that integrates persistent memory into model computation. Through the token-level stable memory updates, Mixture-of-Storage, a deliberate backbone preparation, and a two-stage training pipeline, MemT-1.0 supports efficient storage and utilization of historical information. Both models outperform the evaluated parametric memory baselines on average, while largely preserving the general capabilities of their respective backbones under the noise setting. Applications to coding agents further demonstrate that native memory can internalize procedural experience to improve task success and execution consistency. Future work will focus on improving long-term memory, scaling memory capacity, and reducing the cost of memory updates. We will explore autonomous experience acquisition and continual memory consolidation across tasks, moving toward agents learning through memory-native evolution.

Appendix B Adaptation to Specific Backbones

Table 6 summarizes the memory geometry of the MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash models used in the main evaluations. Both use one memory block per selected layer (E=1E=1). The four-expert MoS workload in Appendix F measures the cost of capacity expansion separately. Layer indices below start at zero.

B.1 Projection and Fusion

MemT-1.0-Nano. MemT-1.0-Nano augments each full-attention layer of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with a native memory block, preserving the original hybrid architecture and MoE computation. The memory branch receives the same pre-normalized hidden states as the original attention and assigns an independent memory channel to each query head. Memory query, key, and value projections are dense and initialized from the corresponding backbone attention projections. The query projection copies the query component of the backbone’s joint query/output-gate projection. The two backbone KV heads are each copied into eight memory heads, giving 16 independently trainable memory heads. The copies share initial values but are separate parameters, with separate channel-wise gates and memory states. After per-head RMSNorm and output gating, the 16 readouts are concatenated into a 4096-dimension vector, added to the backbone’s already-gated attention output, and passed through its frozen ×20484096\!\times\!2048 output projection. The backbone sigmoid gate therefore applies only to the original attention branch, while memory uses the output gate defined in Section 2.

MemT-1.0-Flash. MemT-1.0-Flash attaches a native memory block to the compressed-attention layers of DeepSeek-V4. The backbone compressed-attention has 64 query heads of dimension 512, and the memory branch keeps the same geometry, assigning one independent memory channel to each query head.

The memory query projection follows the backbone query projection, which is a two-stage bottleneck that maps the hidden state of width 4096 to a rank-1024 factor and then to 32768 features. Both stages and the normalization gain on the intermediate factor are copied from the backbone attention. This normalization depends on the input and therefore remains in the projection rather than being folded into the weights.

Keys and values instead use a grouped bottleneck. Eight latent groups of width 512 are projected from the hidden state, and each group is normalized by its own RMSNorm over the group’s 512 features. The group is then expanded to eight heads of dimension 512, so that the eight groups yield 64 memory heads in total, matching the backbone query-head count.

The eight groups are initialized from three backbone projections: the layer’s local KV projection, written LL, and the previous and current halves of the compressed-attention projection, written PP and CC. Group gg draws its key and value from the gg-th entry of the following list of pairings:

(L,L),(P,C),(P,L),(C,P),(C,L),(L,P),(L,C),(C,C).(L,L),\ (P,C),\ (P,L),\ (C,P),\ (C,L),\ (L,P),\ (L,C),\ (C,C).

Here PP and CC denote the two halves of a single backbone projection, and a pairing such as (P,C)(P,C) means that the key is taken from the previous half and the value from the current half. Each group also copies the normalization gain and epsilon of the backbone module that its pairing selects, so groups drawing from LL inherit the local KV normalization while those drawing from PP or CC inherit the compressed-attention normalization. Within a group, the expansion to the eight heads is initialized as an identity mapping and the heads are trained independently.

After readout, the backbone’s frozen grouped output projection maps eight groups of 4096 features to eight groups of 1024. The resulting 8192-dimensional memory contribution is added at the input of the final backbone output projection, which contracts it to the hidden width of 4096. The original backbone residual and hyper-connection operations are preserved.

B.2 Gates and Initialization

All gates take the pre-attention hidden state directly. MemT-1.0-Nano uses dense erase/write projections and rank-256 factorizations for the forget and output gates. MemT-1.0-Flash uses rank-512 factorizations for all four gates. There is no intervening nonlinearity or normalization between gate factors, so the erase/write factors compose into the effective matrices in Section 2. MemT-1.0-Flash’s Q/K/V bottleneck normalization, described above, is distinct from these gate projections.

New gate input weights are initialized from 𝒩⁡(0,0.022)\mathcal{N}(0,0.02^{2}). For both models, the forget-gate expansion starts at zero and the output-gate expansion uses 𝒩⁡(0,0.0012)\mathcal{N}(0,0.001^{2}). MemT-1.0-Nano copies the initial erase projection into the write projection, then trains them independently. MemT-1.0-Flash initializes the erase/write expansion factors independently from 𝒩⁡(0,0.022)\mathcal{N}(0,0.02^{2}) and initializes the output-gate bias to 0.10.1. MemT-1.0-Nano has no output-gate bias. Both use a SoftCapSiLU threshold of 2.02.0 in the evaluated models.

Forget-gate biases encode a range of initial time scales. For each key channel, a half-life τ1/2\tau_{1/2} is sampled independently and log-uniformly from [2048,32768][2048,32768] tokens for MemT-1.0-Nano and [128,32768][128,32768] tokens for MemT-1.0-Flash. We initialize

bλ=Softplus−1⁡(log⁡2τ1/2),sh=0.b_{\lambda}=\operatorname{Softplus}^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\log 2}{\tau_{1/2}}\right),\qquad s_{h}=0.

Together with the zero forget-gate expansion, this sets the initial decay time scale through a factor 2−1/τ1/22^{-1/\tau_{1/2}} per token. Both the channel-wise bias bλb_{\lambda} and head-wise log-scale shs_{h} remain trainable and are excluded from weight decay. Memory states start at zero for each independent trajectory.

B.3 Training Configuration

The trainable parameter counts in Table 6 include memory Q/K/V projections, gate projections and biases, decay scales, and memory normalization gains. Backbone parameters, including the output projections used for fusion, are frozen during memory training. Model parameters and projection computation use BF16. Optimizer master parameters, gradient accumulation/reduction, and Adam moments use FP32. Memory-state accumulation and the sensitive normalization/decay calculations also use FP32.

The single-GPU MoS measurements in Appendix F have their own workload and software configuration.

Setting S0=0S_{0}=0, we obtain

St=∑i=1tΦt:i+1Bi.S_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\Phi_{t:i+1}B_{i}. (3)

Assuming ∥Pt∥≤ρ\lVert P_{t}\rVert\leq\rho and ∥Bt∥≤R\lVert B_{t}\rVert\leq R, an upper bound of ∥St∥\lVert S_{t}\rVert is

∥St∥≤R​∑j=0t−1ρj,\lVert S_{t}\rVert\leq R\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\rho^{j}, (4)

∥St∥≤{R​1−ρt1−ρ,0≤ρ<1,t​R,ρ=1,R​ρt−1ρ−1,ρ>1.\lVert S_{t}\rVert\leq\begin{cases}\displaystyle R\frac{1-\rho^{t}}{1-\rho},&0\leq\rho<1,\\[8.00003pt] \displaystyle tR,&\rho=1,\\[6.00006pt] \displaystyle R\frac{\rho^{t}-1}{\rho-1},&\rho>1.\end{cases} (5)

Therefore, when ρ<1\rho<1, we have ∥St∥≤R1−ρ\lVert S_{t}\rVert\leq\frac{R}{1-\rho} as t→∞t\to\infty, and the update is bounded; we call such a recursion a stable update.

Next, we analyze the vector-form GDN-2 update:

St=(I−kt⊤​(bt⊙kt))​Dt​St−1+kt⊤​(wt⊙vt),S_{t}=\bigl(I-k_{t}^{\top}(b_{t}\odot k_{t})\bigr)D_{t}S_{t-1}+k_{t}^{\top}(w_{t}\odot v_{t}), (6)

where Dt=Diag⁡(dt)D_{t}=\mathrm{Diag}(d_{t}) is diagonal, dt,bt,wt∈(0,1)d_{t},b_{t},w_{t}\in(0,1), and ∥kt∥2=1,∥vt∥2≤g\lVert k_{t}\rVert_{2}=1,\lVert v_{t}\rVert_{2}\leq g, gg is a boundary of vv’s norm.

We omit the time index and define

Then

ρ=∑ibi​ki2,m=∑ibi2​ki2,\rho=\sum_{i}b_{i}k_{i}^{2},\qquad m=\sum_{i}b_{i}^{2}k_{i}^{2}, (8)

and ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), m∈[ρ2,ρ)m\in[\rho^{2},\rho).

Decompose aa into the component parallel to kk and the orthogonal component. Let ee be a unit vector such that e​k⊤=0ek^{\top}=0 and ∥e∥2=1\lVert e\rVert_{2}=1. Define γ2=m−ρ2\gamma^{2}=m-\rho^{2}, then

a=ρ​k+γ​e.a=\rho k+\gamma e. (9)

A=I−k⊤​a=[1−ρ−γ01]⊕IK−2.A=I-k^{\top}a=\begin{bmatrix}1-\rho&-\gamma\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\oplus I_{K-2}. (10)

e​A⊤=e−γ​k,∥e​A⊤∥22=1+γ2≥1.eA^{\top}=e-\gamma k,\qquad\lVert eA^{\top}\rVert_{2}^{2}=1+\gamma^{2}\geq 1. (11)

This shows that along the ee direction, whenever γ≠0\gamma\neq 0, the update amplifies energy, and AA may lead to an unstable recursion. Moreover,

γ=0⇔a|k.\gamma=0\iff a\parallel k. (12)

Thus, if we only consider AA, a prerequisite for stability is that b⊙kb\odot k must be colinear with kk.

We further analyze AA by focusing on its 2×22\times 2 non-trivial block A2A_{2} and considering A2⊤​A2A_{2}^{\top}A_{2}. Its trace is T=2−2​ρ+mT=2-2\rho+m and its determinant is det(A2⊤​A2)=(1−ρ)2\det(A_{2}^{\top}A_{2})=(1-\rho)^{2}. The squared spectral norm (i.e., the largest singular value squared) is

The right-hand side achieves its maximum 43\frac{4}{3} at ρ=13\rho=\frac{1}{3}, hence

1≤∥A∥2<23.1\leq\lVert A\rVert_{2}<\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}. (16)

This gives an upper bound on the spectral norm of AA. When both AA and DD are considered in the update, if ∥D∥2≤d¯\lVert D\rVert_{2}\leq\overline{d}, then

∥P∥2=∥A​D∥2≤23​d¯.\lVert P\rVert_{2}=\lVert AD\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,\overline{d}. (17)

To ensure uniform contraction bound for PtP_{t} less than 1, a sufficient condition is d¯<32≈0.866\overline{d}<\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\approx 0.866. Since Pt​St−1P_{t}S_{t-1} does not always amplify, d¯<0.866\overline{d}<0.866 is a sufficient condition for stability in the worst case. This condition guaranties uniform contraction of the homogeneous recursion. If the additive inputs Bt=kt⊤​(wt⊙vt)B_{t}=k_{t}^{\top}(w_{t}\odot v_{t}) are uniformly bounded, then the resulting inhomogeneous recursion is uniformly bounded as well. Under this condition, the half-life of the forget gate DD,

t1/2=ln⁡2−ln⁡d=ln⁡2−ln3/2≈4.82,t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{-\ln d}=\frac{\ln 2}{-\ln\sqrt{3}/{2}}\approx 4.82, (18)

is only about 5 tokens.

C.2 Solution: Symmetrization Fix

Note that in the GDN-2 update, the AA term can be written as

A=I−k⊤​(b⊙k)=I−k⊤​k​Diag​(b).A=I-k^{\top}(b\odot k)=I-k^{\top}k\,\mathrm{Diag}(b). (19)

The instability stems from the fact that AA is not symmetric. We therefore move Diag⁡(b)\mathrm{Diag}(b) to both kk to make AA symmetric:

A=I−Diag​(b)​k⊤​k​Diag​(b).A=I-\text{Diag}(\sqrt{b})\,k^{\top}k\,\text{Diag}(\sqrt{b}). (20)

Further, we can rewrite it as

A=I−(b⊙k)⊤​(b⊙k).A=I-(\sqrt{b}\odot k)^{\top}(\sqrt{b}\odot k). (21)

With this symmetrization fix, we obtain Stable GDN-2 (SGDN-2), whose update is

St=(I−(bt⊙kt)⊤​(bt⊙kt))​Dt​St−1+(bt⊙kt)⊤​(wt⊙vt).S_{t}=\bigl(I-(\sqrt{b_{t}}\odot k_{t})^{\top}(\sqrt{b_{t}}\odot k_{t})\bigr)D_{t}S_{t-1}+(\sqrt{b_{t}}\odot k_{t})^{\top}(w_{t}\odot v_{t}). (22)

According to the analysis above, the two vectors in SGDN-2 are naturally colinear (i.e., γ=0\gamma=0), which avoids the unstable update mechanism.

Geometrically, the symmetrized erase step acts separately on the component parallel to u=b⊙ku=\sqrt{b}\odot k and its orthogonal complement, with no coupling between these two orthogonal subspaces. Considering the erase step alone, with D=ID=I and no write term, the parallel component is scaled by 1−∥u∥221-\lVert u\rVert_{2}^{2}, while the orthogonal component remains unchanged. Under the stated assumptions, 0<∥u∥22<10<\lVert u\rVert_{2}^{2}<1; hence, the map contracts along uu without expanding any orthogonal direction and is non-expansive in the Euclidean norm.

In contrast, GDN-2 computes the erase magnitude using a=b⊙ka=b\odot k but applies the correction along kk. For the input y=ey=e, this gives y′=e−γ​ky^{\prime}=e-\gamma k. Since ee and kk are orthogonal, the correction increases the squared norm from 11 to 1+γ21+\gamma^{2} whenever γ≠0\gamma\neq 0. Figure 12 illustrates the resulting non-expansive map and contrasts it with a GDN-2 erase step that increases the norm of the same input y=ey=e.

Appendix D Details of Evaluation Setup

D.1 Details of Benchmarks

Memory Benchmark. We evaluate memory capabilities on 11 benchmarks and divide them into four groups according to trajectory length as follows. These benchmarks focus on long-term information retention and retrieval, dynamic memory updating and management, and personalized understanding.
∙\bullet MemBench [27]: MemBench reports the equal-weight mean accuracy across its factual/reflective and participation/observation quadrants on the 0–10K subset. We write each history in an independent scope and preserve its original message order. We note that when structured time is unavailable, no synthetic date is constructed.
∙\bullet ImplicitMemBench [28]: ImplicitMemBench evaluates procedural learning, priming, and classical conditioning through learning or priming, interference, and test stages. We preserve the original trajectory order, isolate priming treatment and control groups. Specifically, we use temperature 0.8 for the priming task.
∙\bullet PersonaMem [29]: PersonaMem evaluates dynamic user profiling and personalized responses over evolving interactions. Each (history, history_end) pair receives an independent scope. Questions with the same cutoff share a read-only state, whereas different cutoffs do not share memory. We utilize the 32K length subset of PersonaMem for our memory evaluation.
∙\bullet PS-Bench [30]: PS-Bench measures whether personal memories induce intent legitimation and increase personalized attack success. Persona histories follow the original session, speaker, and timestamp order. We report 100​(1−ASR)100(1-\mathrm{ASR}) on the Persona-grounded subset, with ASR micro-averaged over 1,863 queries.
∙\bullet LoCoMo [31]: LoCoMo evaluates single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and adversarial conversational memory. We preserve session, message, speaker, and date order. We also use speaker-specific scopes for MemOS, Mem0, and Graphiti, and use a conversation scope for OpenViking. We exclude the adversarial category from the reported score.
∙\bullet PerMemSafe [32]: PerMemSafe evaluates implicit personalized safety through Safety Perception (SP) and Dynamic Evolution (DE) tracks. SP and DE histories use independent scopes, while risk descriptions, isolated answers, and scoring rubrics are excluded from memory writes. Specifically, we utilize the conv64 subset of PerMemSafe in our memory evaluation.
∙\bullet Memora [33]: Memora evaluates remembering, reasoning, and recommendation under evolving weekly, monthly, and quarterly interactions. Each persona uses an independent scope with chronological session and turn writes and timestamps. Query dates are not used to filter history. We utilize the Weekly subset of Memora for memory evaluation.
∙\bullet MemOps [34]: MemOps evaluates remembering, updating, forgetting, reflecting, and composed memory operations. We store 50 sessions by session index and message order in an independent scope, excluding operation labels, state annotations, and provenance tags from memory.
∙\bullet LongMemEval [35]: LongMemEval evaluates information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, and abstention. Each haystack uses an independent scope and session-date order, and the current date appears only in the query and is not stored in memory. We utilize the LongMemEval-S subset for our memory evaluation.
∙\bullet MemoryAgentBench [36]: MemoryAgentBench evaluates retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and selective forgetting. Source histories are isolated and written in complete chunk-N order without source mixing. The main set is used, excluding the short-context ablation questions.
∙\bullet BEAM [37]: BEAM evaluates ten long-context memory abilities, including extraction, contradiction resolution, updating, preference following, summarization, and temporal reasoning. Each conversation uses an independent scope and complete chronological writes by session, timestamp, and message. We utilize the 1M subset of BEAM for our memory evaluation. Due to the limitation of generation, the full context retains at most the latest 256K tokens.

General Benchmark. We evaluate general capabilities on six benchmarks spanning four major dimensions: knowledge and scientific reasoning, instruction following, long-context understanding, and code generation. The detailed benchmarks are presented as follows.

∙\bullet MMLU-Pro [38]: MMLU-Pro extends MMLU with harder reasoning questions and ten answer choices. We use the TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro@14be195 test split and evaluate these conditions with fixed demonstrations provided through ordinary context or native memory.
∙\bullet GPQA Diamond [39]: GPQA Diamond contains graduate-level biology, physics, and chemistry questions designed to resist ordinary web search. We evaluate each of the 198 questions eight times, keeping its answer-option order fixed across repetitions and evaluation conditions, and report mean accuracy.
∙\bullet IFEval [40]: IFEval evaluates programmatically verifiable constraints such as length, keywords, casing, and formatting. We use the 541-prompt, 834-instruction test split and provide fixed irrelevant demonstrations through ordinary context or native memory.
∙\bullet LongBench v2 [41]: LongBench v2 evaluates deep reasoning across six long-context task categories and contexts up to 2M words. We use the 503-item train split and provide identical irrelevant demonstrations through ordinary context or native memory.
∙\bullet BigCodeBench-Hard [42]: BigCodeBench-Hard contains 148 practical programming tasks with complex instructions and function calls. We use normalized v0.1.4 test data, execute generated programs with the official tests, and report Pass@1 under the evaluated configurations.
∙\bullet LiveCodeBench v6 [43]: LiveCodeBench is a continuously refreshed coding benchmark based on recent LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces problems. We use the 1,055-item cumulative release_v6 split and preserve identical demonstrations, generation settings, and scoring protocols across conditions.

D.2 Details of Baselines

We compare MemT-1.0 with textual and parametric memory baselines as follows. Methods with the same backbones share prompts, generation settings, and scoring protocols.

∙\bullet Full Context: Full context prepends the available history to the query as a context-only reference. Histories exceeding the 256K-token local window are left-truncated, retaining the most recent visible tokens.
∙\bullet DenseRAG: DenseRAG retrieves the 10 most relevant historical segments and prepends them to the query. In our implementation, the retrieval process is scope-isolated, and LoCoMo segments are indexed as Speaker said, ‘‘text’’, and answers are not written back.
∙\bullet MemOS [45]: MemOS provides structured extraction, synchronization, and hybrid memory retrieval. We use version 2.0.32 with multimodal_struct, fine, and sync, top-20 fast search, MMR deduplication, and reranking.
∙\bullet Mem0 [46]: Mem0 performs LLM-based memory extraction, updating, and semantic retrieval. We use version 2.0.20 with infer=true, dataset-specific protective chunking, top-20 user-scoped retrieval, and reranking disabled.
∙\bullet OpenViking [47]: OpenViking organizes session-level memories hierarchically for retrieval. We use version 0.4.17.1 with a 32,768-token submission budget and retain the top 20 user-scoped contexts without additional reranking.
∙\bullet Graphiti [48]: Graphiti represents memory as a temporal knowledge graph. We use version 0.30.1, dataset-specific Episode boundaries, and EDGE hybrid RRF to retrieve the top-20 facts within the current group.
∙\bullet Temp-LoRA [49]: Temp-LoRA adapts model parameters separately for each history. We train a rank-64 temporary LoRA on non-overlapping 1,024-token chunks for two epochs per chunk. We use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as its backbone.
∙\bullet Doc-to-LoRA [50]: Doc-to-LoRA maps document chunks into lightweight parameter updates. Using public Qwen3-4B weights, we generate rank-8 down_proj LoRAs and retain only the final three chunk adapters.
∙\bullet SHINE [51]: SHINE encodes historical information as generated low-rank parameter updates. We use public Qwen3-8B weights and rank-8 LoRAs on all linear layers. We use the full history when it contains at most 2,380 tokens. Otherwise, we retain only the last 2,380 tokens before generating the LoRA.
∙\bullet δ\delta-mem [52]: δ\delta-mem maintains a recurrent memory state updated during inference. We use the rank-8 Qwen3-4B TSW adapter and write each history into its online state token by token.
∙\bullet LiveMem [53]: We choose LiveMem-RL, which maintains a recurrent state while releasing historical key-value caches after writing. We use its Qwen3-4B implementation and retain the latest 257K tokens on MemoryAgentBench.
∙\bullet MemoryLLM [54]: MemoryLLM stores history in a fixed pool of learned memory vectors. We use MemoryLLM-8B-Chat with 12,800 vectors per layer and a 2,048-token query window, completing 1,993 MemoryAgentBench questions.
∙\bullet ICAE [55]: ICAE compresses each segment into continuous latent slots. We use Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, 128 slots per segment, and FIFO retention of four segments; this differs from the original SpanExtrap setting.

For the retrieval processes, Graphiti, Mem0, MemOS, and OpenViking use BGE-M3 embeddings and the corresponding DeepSeek or Qwen3.6 branch model for extraction and answering. We disable the thinking mode of Qwen3.6. When Graphiti or Mem0 extraction calls are blocked, they fall back to the local Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model.

D.3 Details of Pipelines and Prompts in Memory Evaluation

D.3.1 Query Prompt Construction

We do not add generic few-shot demonstrations to the memory benchmarks. For the full context, the visible history and the current query are included in the same request. When a history exceeds the local context limit of 256K tokens, we retain its most recent suffix. For parametric memory methods, the history is first written through the protocol supported by the method. At query time, the model receives only the task instruction and the current question, without a second copy of the history. For external memory systems, retrieved memories from the current scope are inserted into a fixed answer template. Within each benchmark, Graphiti, Mem0, MemOS, and OpenViking use the same answer template and differ only in the retrieved content. Gold answers, evidence identifiers, and scoring labels are never included in the answering-model input.

The principal English query templates are given below. Braced expressions denote fields instantiated from each evaluation example at runtime. Unless stated otherwise, the templates shown first are those used by the full context models.

The second instruction is included only for Event Ordering and is omitted for all other BEAM-1M capabilities.

Memory-query adaptation and retrieval-template construction. The full context setting retains each dataset’s original references to the history. After a memory method has written the history, however, the query message no longer contains the history body. We therefore replace only statements that would incorrectly claim that the history remains in the current prompt. The question, answer choices, output format, and all other task instructions remain unchanged. For Graphiti, Mem0, MemOS, and OpenViking, these adaptations are combined with a benchmark-frozen retrieval template. All four systems use the same template for a given benchmark; only the entries represented by [Memory N] differ. The resulting construction for each benchmark is described below.

LoCoMo. For memory-based evaluation, “Below is a conversation between two people. Answer the question using only this conversation.” is replaced by “Answer the question using only the conversation stored in your memory.” In the external-memory version, the retrieved content is introduced by “Below are retrieved memories from a conversation between two people.” Open-ended questions require a brief answer, whereas multiple-choice questions require only (a) or (b).

LongMemEval-S. The opening instruction is changed from “I will give you several history chats between you and a user. Please answer the question based on the relevant chat history.” to “Answer the question based on the relevant chat history stored in your memory.” The empty History Chats: block is removed. For external memory systems, the query contains Retrieved Memory Chats, the current date, the question, and an Answer: cue.

MemBench. For participation tasks, the opening instruction becomes “Answer the multiple-choice question using only the conversation stored in your memory.” For observation tasks, it becomes “Answer the multiple-choice question using only the observations stored in your memory.” The empty History: block is removed in both cases. The external-memory query contains a Retrieved memories section followed by the current time, the question, and answer choices A–D, and requires only the option letter.

PersonaMem-32K. The original query does not state that the history appears in the current prompt, so removing the history body requires no additional wording change. For external memory systems, the query contains the retrieved memories, the question, four candidate responses, and the original <final_answer> constraint.

PS-Bench. No query-stem replacement is required after the history body is removed. The external-memory query combines the natural-tone instruction, the retrieved memories, and the current user input. Base questions omit the memory section because they are evaluated with an empty state.

PerMemSafe-conv64. No additional query-stem replacement is required. The system message remains “You are a helpful assistant.”, and the external-memory user message contains the retrieved memories followed by the current question.

Memora Weekly. Statements asserting that the history is supplied in the current prompt are changed consistently to state that it is stored in and accessible from memory. Specifically, “The conversation history below contains ALL your previous conversations with this user—this history is PROVIDED TO YOU in this prompt” becomes “Your memory contains ALL previous conversations with this user”; “conversation history that is provided below” becomes “conversation history stored in memory”; “The conversation history is PROVIDED IN THIS PROMPT—you have full access to it” becomes “The conversation history is stored in memory—you have access to it”; and “because the history is right here in this prompt” becomes “because the history is available in memory.” For external memory systems, the system instruction requires the answer to rely only on retrieved memories and to use the most recent value. The user message contains # Retrieved Memories followed by # Current Question.

MemOps. “I will give you conversation history between you and a user. Answer based only on the provided conversation context.” is replaced by “Answer based only on the conversation history stored in your memory.” The phrase “transition reasoning over the provided context” becomes “transition reasoning over that memory”; “If the context does not contain enough information” becomes “If your memory does not contain enough information”; and “If the history contains an instruction to forget or update a fact” becomes “If your memory contains an instruction to forget or update a fact.” The empty Conversation Context: block is removed. The external-memory query retains the operation-detection and forget-redaction instructions and contains a Retrieved Memory Context section, optional candidate choices, the question, and the JSON: output cue.

ImplicitMemBench. Removing the history body requires no additional wording change. In the external-memory template, Retrieved memories is followed directly by the Current probe; the expected response pattern and scoring rubric are not included.

MemoryAgentBench. Removing the history body requires no additional wording change. The external-memory query retains the fixed system message, describes the retrieved memories according to the source family, and appends the corresponding source-specific query.

BEAM-1M. Removing the history body requires no additional wording change. The external-memory template contains # CONTEXT, # INSTRUCTIONS, # QUESTION, and # ANSWER. Event Ordering additionally requires one event per line in chronological order.

D.3.2 Decoding Configuration

All formal comparisons use the same decoding configuration for every method and condition within a given benchmark. The only exception is the Priming subtask of ImplicitMemBench, for which the temperature is set to 0.80.8. All other tasks use temperature 00. The Qwen3.6 branch disables Thinking for every request. The DeepSeek branch uses the official chat template and verifies before evaluation that Thinking is disabled. The model context window is limited to 256K tokens, and chunked prefilling uses a chunk size of 8,192 tokens. If generation reaches the benchmark-specific maximum length without producing an end-of-sequence token, we retain the sample and score the actual generated output rather than discarding it.

The maximum generation length is benchmark-specific. LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S use a maximum of 512 tokens, while MemBench uses a maximum of 16 tokens. PS-Bench uses a maximum of 512 tokens. PersonaMem-32K uses a maximum of 2,048 tokens. MemOps, PerMemSafe-conv64, and Memora Weekly also use a maximum of 2,048 tokens. ImplicitMemBench uses a maximum of 4,096 tokens.

For BEAM-1M, the maximum depends on the capability being evaluated. Abstention, Information Extraction, Knowledge Update, and Temporal Reasoning use 512 tokens. Contradiction Resolution, Instruction Following, Multi-session Reasoning, and Preference Following use 1,024 tokens. Event Ordering uses 2,048 tokens, and Summarization uses 4,096 tokens.

For MemoryAgentBench, the maximum is source- and task-specific. RULER QA uses 50 tokens, EventQA uses 40 tokens, the LongMemEval-S source uses 50 tokens, recommendation tasks use 300 tokens, and ICL tasks use 20 tokens. The maximum is 1,200 tokens for summarization, 2,000 tokens for DetectiveQA, and 10 tokens for FactConsolidation.

D.4 Details of Pipelines and Prompts in General Evaluation

Reasoning modes, sampling, and context construction. All evaluation configurations within a benchmark use the same prompt version, parser, scorer, and corresponding implementation version. General-capability evaluations use Thinking mode for both the DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B branches. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, we set reasoning_effort=high, temperature to 1.01.0, top_p to 1.01.0, and presence penalty to 0.00.0. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MemT-1.0-Flash use a maximum output budget of 131,072 tokens within a total context window of 262,144 tokens, with the output budget adjusted to the remaining context capacity. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, we set temperature to 1.01.0, top_p to 0.950.95, top_k to 2020, min_p to 0.00.0, presence penalty to 1.51.5, and repetition penalty to 1.01.0. The Qwen branch uses a maximum output budget of 81,920 tokens. Both output budgets include reasoning and answer tokens.

The Qwen branch uses its native 262,144-token context window for all tasks except LongBench v2. For Qwen on LongBench v2, we use the official YaRN configuration with an expansion factor of 44, yielding an effective context window of 1,010,000 tokens. For LongBench v2, target inputs follow the official middle-truncation procedure. For the backbone noise condition, the fixed demonstrations are added after this truncation and are excluded from the target-input truncation. The native-memory condition uses the same truncated target input. The generation budgets above replace the source implementations’ default output limits; LongBench v2 retains its official prompt construction, intermediate truncation, answer extraction, and scoring rules.

The fixed demonstrations provide the irrelevant information used in the noise setting described in Section 6.3. They consist of question–answer examples whose primary capability differs from that of the target benchmark. Specifically, we use three BigCodeBench-Hard examples for MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond, and ten AIME 2026 examples for IFEval, LongBench v2, BigCodeBench-Hard, and LiveCodeBench v6. Each demonstration set contains fewer than 2,048 tokens. For each benchmark, the same examples are prepended to the backbone’s input context or written into an initially empty MemT-1.0 memory state in a single commit before evaluation. Each question independently reads the resulting state, which remains fixed during evaluation. Selection is independent of model outputs and evaluation scores and excludes target questions, direct rewrites of target answers, and native few-shot examples.

MMLU-Pro. We use the official subject-specific five-shot chain-of-thought prompt. The model answer is parsed only when an explicit answer marker is followed by an option from A–J or when an A–J option appears on a separate line. We report micro-averaged accuracy. Unparseable answers and answers containing mutually conflicting choices are counted as incorrect.

GPQA Diamond. For each underlying question, we evaluate it eight times using a fixed answer-option order. Every evaluation condition shares exactly the same option orders. We first aggregate the eight responses within each underlying question and then compute accuracy over the 198 underlying questions.

IFEval. We retain the dataset’s original prompts and add no task-level few-shot examples. The official programmatic constraint checker is applied to every instruction. We report prompt-level strict accuracy, counting a prompt as correct only when all of its associated constraints are satisfied.

LongBench v2. We use the official zero-shot direct-answer prompt. Inputs longer than 120,000 tokens are truncated according to the official middle-truncation procedure using the o200k_base tokenizer. Answers are extracted with the official implementation at commit c5ea10b, and we report accuracy.

BigCodeBench-Hard. We use the v0.1.4 Hard/Instruct tasks without prefilled code and generate one candidate solution per task. Each candidate is executed in the official BigCodeBench v0.2.4 container. We report Pass@1. Execution failures and outputs containing no valid code are counted as incorrect.

LiveCodeBench v6. We use the cumulative release_v6 test split and the official code generation prompt, generating one candidate solution per problem. Candidates are executed with the official LiveCodeBench runner at commit 28fef95. We report Pass@1, counting execution failures and outputs without valid code as incorrect.

All conditions within a benchmark use the same task prompts, demonstration selection, parsing rules, scorer versions, and execution settings. Programmatic checks and code execution are performed with the frozen versions specified above. Empty outputs, generation failures, and unparseable answers remain in the predetermined denominator and are assigned the failure outcome defined by the corresponding benchmark.

D.5 Details of Storage Overhead Evaluation

For the storage overhead evaluation, note that process-level max_memory_allocated includes model weights and memory pools, and therefore does not reflect the per-session storage overhead.

For full-context inference, we report the logical state size after history preparation and before querying. The storage grows linearly with the visible context length and is capped at 256K tokens on BEAM. DenseRAG stores FP32 retrieval vectors together with their corresponding chunk texts. Temp-LoRA stores the query-time BF16 adapter while excluding optimizer states. MemT-1.0 stores a full-rank memory state.

Appendix E Additional Details on Agentic Tasks

E.1 Experience Bank and Training Data Construction

E.1.1 Experience Bank Construction

We construct the experience bank in four stages. First, we treat each trajectory as an episode and annotate it with its key decisions and a state signature comprising topic tags, the first tool used, and the error code. Second, episodes with the same state signature are pooled, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro [16] induces a policy of the form “when condition XX holds, take action YY, verify with ZZ, and watch out for WW” from each pool. Each policy must specify a trigger observable from the agent’s state. Source-specific entities such as repository, product, and file names are abstracted into variables. Third, policies describing the same workflow are clustered based on the lexical similarity of their titles, triggers, and procedures, with one policy retained as the representative of each cluster. Finally, DeepSeek-V4-Pro synthesizes a structured experience from the trajectories supporting each representative policy. An automated check verifies that the declared tools appear in the supporting trajectories, and a separate LLM audit filters out experiences containing severe errors.

We summarize the construction funnel and the resulting experience bank in Table 8. Each experience contains ten fields, including a retrieval description to support matching, a trigger context specifying when it applies, steps and parameters specifying what to do, preconditions defining its scope of applicability, and decision guidance documenting preferred choices and potential pitfalls.

Most experiences are specific, since 942 of the 1,040 derive from a single trajectory, while a few broad workflows draw on hundreds. The bank emphasizes procedural guidance and verification, with verification and testing-related tags among the most frequent after the python tag. Issue-level retrieval provides limited discrimination among top-ranked candidates: the median difference in similarity scores between the first- and fifth-ranked candidates is only 0.029.

E.1.2 Experience-Conditioned Trajectory Construction

We construct experience-conditioned training trajectories in five stages, as demonstrated in Figure 13: generating original trajectories, identifying candidate breakpoints, selecting and injecting experiences, validating the intervention outcomes, and serializing the resulting training examples.

We represent an agent trajectory as

ξ=(h0,a0,o0,…,hT,aT,oT),\xi=\left(h_{0},a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,h_{T},a_{T},o_{T}\right),

where hth_{t}, ata_{t}, and oto_{t} denote the interaction history before step tt, the action produced by the agent, and the corresponding environment observation, respectively.

Breakpoint Identification

For unsuccessful trajectories, we sequentially scan the observations in each rollout. A step tt is marked as a candidate breakpoint based on execution feedback, including command failures, empty observations after normalization, and repeated unsuccessful operations. This criterion relies only on feedback visible to the agent at execution time and does not access reference solutions or privileged evaluation information.

To prevent long trajectories from producing a disproportionate number of intervention variants, we retain at most eight breakpoints per rollout. If a rollout contains more than eight candidates, we sample eight of them without replacement using a fixed random seed. We additionally record the total number of candidate breakpoints and the positions of the retained breakpoints to ensure reproducibility. The Harness-Triggered evaluation setting uses the same breakpoint-detection logic, with at most one experience store operation per trajectory. Before Execution evaluates robustness to experience injection timing.

Experience Retrieval and Counterfactual Validation

For each task, we first retrieve the top-10 most relevant entries from the experience bank. We then construct ten candidate experience subsets for every retained breakpoint: one subset containing the complete top-3 entries, one containing the complete top-5 entries, and eight three-entry subsets sampled from the top-10 retrieved entries. Random sampling is performed using a fixed seed associated with each task instance.

Each breakpoint-experience-subset pair defines an independent continuation rollout. The resulting intervention trajectory is

ξb,j=ξ≤b⊕[gb,j]⊕ξ^>b(gb,j).\xi_{b,j}=\xi_{\leq b}\oplus[g_{b,j}]\oplus\hat{\xi}_{>b}^{(g_{b,j})}.

Here, bb indexes the selected breakpoint, jj indexes the candidate experience subset, and ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation of message sequences. We retain a trajectory as a training sample if and only if

{Success⁡(ξ)=0,Success⁡(ξb,j)=1,\begin{cases}\operatorname{Success}(\xi)=0,\\ \operatorname{Success}(\xi_{b,j})=1,\end{cases}

which means the original trajectory must fail to solve the task, whereas the experience-conditioned continuation must pass the task tests. Variants that fail the tests, terminate abnormally, or cannot be reproduced are excluded from the training set.

Training Sample Serialization

Finally, each training sample is serialized as

xb,j=(ξ≤b,gb,j,ξ^>b+(gb,j)),x_{b,j}=\left(\xi_{\leq b},g_{b,j},\hat{\xi}_{>b}^{+\left(g_{b,j}\right)}\right),

where the three components correspond to the triggering execution state, the experience subset, and the successful continuation suffix, respectively. The superscript ++ indicates that the generated suffix passes the task evaluation.

E.1.3 Dataset Statistics and Splits

We partition the constructed data into training and validation sets by task, keeping all original rollouts, breakpoints, and intervention variants associated with each task in the same split, and SWE-bench Verified serves as the test set. We report the number of tasks and repositories of each split in Table 9.

Throughout data construction, we check breakpoint validity, consistency between trajectory prefixes and repository snapshots, test outcomes, message and tool-call structure, and context length. We exclude samples with environment failures, incomplete logs, test-file modifications, other invalid execution behaviors, or outcomes that cannot be reproduced. Samples that exceed the context-length limit or fail structural checks are discarded in full rather than truncated. The scale of the resulting data construction process and the outcomes of experience intervention are reported in Table 10.

E.2 Training Details

We compare training configurations along three dimensions: the objective (CE or KD), the supervision scope (First-Step or Full-Suffix), and the number of successful training trajectories selected per task. Max-2 and Max-3 retain at most two and three successful training trajectories per task, respectively.

E.2.1 Trainable Parameters and Memory Operations

We train Metis on hyper memory blocks at decoder layers ℓ∈{3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39}\ell\in\{3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39\}. Each block contains 10 trainable tensors: W_k.weight, W_v.weight, pool_score.weight, gated_delta_alpha.weight, gated_delta_alpha.bias, gated_delta_beta.weight, gated_delta_beta.bias, query_proj.weight, query_norm.weight, and mem_norm.weight. This gives 100 tensors and 104,962,580 trainable parameters in total, roughly 0.3% of the backbone’s parameter count. The backbone runs in BF16, whereas the memory computation, state accumulation, and all trainable parameters are kept in FP32.

Each memory block maintains a fixed-size memory consisting of a 512×512512\times 512 value state and a 512×1512\times 1 key normalizer, so the memory footprint does not grow with the length of the experience. The key and value projections map the hidden states of the experience to 512-dimensional vectors, while the query projection maps the hidden states of the main trajectory to memory queries. On the write side, the token selector applies alpha top-pp selection with p=0.9p=0.9 and always retains at least one token; the delta update ratio is set to 0.9. On the read side, the memory readout is normalized by mem_norm and fused with the backbone representation using a fusion coefficient of γ=0.9\gamma=0.9. Runtime memory is not retained across tasks. The checkpoint contains only the trainable memory parameters listed above, and every new task or trajectory starts from an empty memory state.

E.2.2 Sample Serialization and Supervision Masks

Each training sample corresponds to exactly one write event, and the memory is reset to empty at the start of every sample. Within a sample, tokens are split into two attention domains: the experience domain, which contains the experience text, and the main domain, which contains the trajectory prefix and the successful continuation. The main domain does not attend to the experience domain, so the experience can influence the main trajectory only through memory.

Replay then proceeds in three stages, which mirror the injection of experience at an execution breakpoint: (1) write: the experience is stored in memory at the end of the experience segment; (2) prefix replay: the main-trajectory prefix is processed with memory reading disabled; and (3) continuation replay: memory reading is enabled from the breakpoint onward, so that all subsequent predictions can access the experience-derived state MM. Consequently, the prediction of the first supervised token is already conditioned on the stored memory. In the training configuration, the write offset is set to zero and no query store operation is performed.

Supervision Settings

Within this replay procedure, we consider two supervision settings. They differ in how much of the successful suffix is supervised and in where the sequence is truncated. Both are trained with teacher forcing on the original token sequences.

Full-Suffix. The loss covers every assistant turn in the successful suffix. For each such turn, the target comprises all tokens following the assistant role header: the reasoning text, the response body, the tool calls, the structural tokens that delimit them, and the closing <|im_end|>\n. All other tokens serve only as conditioning information. These include the experience, the prefix, the role headers, tool responses, and user and system messages. Because training is teacher-forced, each later assistant turn is conditioned on the ground-truth tool responses recorded in the original trajectory, rather than on the results of executing the model’s own actions.

First-Step. The loss covers only the first assistant turn after the breakpoint, focusing supervision on the immediate continuation. We derive these samples from Full-Suffix trajectories whose assistant turns contain reasoning text. For each trajectory, we select the first assistant turn of the successful suffix and truncate the sequence immediately after the closing <|im_end|>\n of this turn. The model input therefore consists of the experience (written to memory), the full prefix, and the selected turn.

Under teacher forcing, every token of the selected turn is predicted from the ground-truth tokens that precede it rather than from tokens generated by the model. The loss is computed only over this turn, using the same target definition as in Full-Suffix. Because truncation removes only trailing tokens, the breakpoint position and the original token IDs remain unchanged, and no re-tokenization is required.

E.2.3 Training Objectives and Hyperparameters

We consider two training objectives: hard-label cross-entropy (CE), and knowledge distillation (KD). The student accesses experience only through native memory, the teacher uses the same frozen backbone with the memory modules disabled and receives the experience as text in prefix–experience–suffix order. Both models use teacher forcing on the same successful continuation, with teacher and student predictions aligned by target token rather than absolute input position.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote the valid supervised positions across all ranks and gradient-accumulation microbatches in one optimizer step, excluding padding, and let N=|𝒯|N=|\mathcal{T}|. For each position tt, let yty_{t} be the target token and let ptS=softmax⁡(ztS)p_{t}^{\mathrm{S}}=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{S}}) be the student distribution over the full vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. We use temperature τ=1\tau=1 throughout.

CE. We minimize the negative log-likelihood of the recorded target tokens:

ℒCE=−1N∑t∈𝒯logpt,ytS.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\log p_{t,y_{t}}^{\mathrm{S}}.

KD. At each supervised position, we retain the K=64K=64 tokens with the largest teacher logits, denoted by 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t}, and renormalize the teacher distribution over this set:

qt,vT=exp⁡(zt,vT)∑u∈𝒦texp⁡(zt,uT),v∈𝒦t.q_{t,v}^{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{\exp(z_{t,v}^{\mathrm{T}})}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{K}_{t}}\exp(z_{t,u}^{\mathrm{T}})},\qquad v\in\mathcal{K}_{t}.

The distillation objective is

ℒKD=1N​∑t∈𝒯∑v∈𝒦tqt,vT​log⁡qt,vTpt,vS.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{K}_{t}}q_{t,v}^{\mathrm{T}}\log\frac{q_{t,v}^{\mathrm{T}}}{p_{t,v}^{\mathrm{S}}}.

Only the teacher distribution is truncated; the student remains normalized over the full vocabulary. This objective transfers experience-conditioned predictions from the textual-context teacher to the memory-conditioned student.

The training and validation sets are split by task, so no task appears in both.

Training uses task interleaving. Unpacked records are replayed for three epochs, and within each epoch they are arranged in a task-interleaved order determined by a fixed base seed combined with the epoch index.

For the Full-Suffix-Max3 run, we additionally use sequence packing to improve training throughput. Packs are first constructed with a fixed seed, without splitting any trajectory across packs, and are then scheduled in a deterministic order. Each pack contains at most 131,072 tokens. Trajectories in the same pack do not share memory: the memory is reset, written, and read independently for each trajectory. Because every step of the schedule is determined by fixed seeds, the data order of each run is fully reproducible.

Each microbatch on a given rank contains exactly one trajectory or one complete pack. Padding slots are assigned a supervised-token count of zero, which ensures that each valid supervised token is counted exactly once in loss normalization. We optimize with AdamW, using FP32 optimizer states sharded across ranks, a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, and three warmup steps.

E.2.4 Training Diagnostics

We compare CE and KD across four paired training configurations, combining First-Step or Full-Suffix supervision with the Max-2 or Max-3 data setting. Within each pair, initialization, training data, and optimization hyperparameters are matched. CE and KD optimize different objectives, so their training losses are not directly comparable. We therefore monitor hard-label validation negative log-likelihood (NLL) for both. Validation comparisons are made within the same supervision scope and data setting.

Optimization and Validation Behavior.

Figure 14 shows decreasing validation NLL under both objectives, with most of the reduction occurring within the first 40 optimizer steps. CE achieves lower final validation NLL than KD in all four paired configurations (Table 11). For Full-Suffix-Max2, CE reduces body-token NLL from 0.2925 to 0.1866, compared with 0.2910 under KD. The same pattern holds for tool-call tokens (0.0603 to 0.0461 under CE versus 0.0545 under KD) and reasoning tokens (0.5033 to 0.4555 versus 0.4749).

Relation to Agent Performance.

KD achieves higher average success rates than CE despite its higher validation NLL (Table 11). For example, Full-Suffix-Max2 records a preliminary success rate of 37.5% under CE, compared with 54.3% under KD, while its validation NLL is lower under CE (0.1795 versus 0.2005). The other three configurations exhibit the same qualitative pattern. These results motivate our selection of KD for all subsequent agent evaluations and ablations. We use validation NLL to monitor optimization, while selecting among KD configurations through repeated agent executions.

E.3 Additional Results

E.3.1 Training Configuration Comparison

Training Configurations.

In Table 12, we compare four Metis KD configurations on the 100-task development subset of SWE-bench Verified under the Before Execution setting, with three runs per task. This subset is included in the full 500-task SWE-bench Verified evaluation reported in the main text. Full-Suffix-Max2 achieves the highest average success and ties for the highest pass@3 and pass^3, motivating its selection for full-benchmark Metis evaluations.

Full-Benchmark Comparison.

In Figure 15, we compare Metis and MemT-1.0-Nano with the backbone and textual-experience baselines on SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks) and SWE-bench Multilingual (300 tasks). Both memory models improve average success and pass^3 over the backbone. Relative to Metis, MemT-1.0-Nano has higher pass@3 but lower pass^3 in all four settings.

E.3.2 Experience Selection

We compare Textual Experience selection strategies on SWE-bench Multilingual (Table 13). Fixed Rank-kk uses the single experience at retrieval rank kk. Per-Task Best selects among three candidates by the number of successful runs, breaking ties by retrieval rank. Since the same runs are used for selection and reporting, it serves as an outcome-selected reference. Rank-1 achieves the highest average success under Before Execution, whereas Rank-2 performs best under Harness-Triggered. Per-Task Best outperforms the fixed-rank strategies in both settings, suggesting that improved experience selection could further benefit task performance.

Appendix F Memory Windowing Experiment

F.1 Experimental Setup

The experiment compares two execution schedules for one standalone MoS memory block. Whole-pack execution produces expert projections for all tokens at once; windowed execution groups complete steps, performs their projections, state updates, and readout in sequence, and recomputes internal intermediates during backward. Both use the same equations, weights, inputs, precision, and update kernel. Measurement covers both routers, all expert projections, memory writes and reads, RMSNorm, SoftCapSiLU, fusion, and backward through these computations.

Each pack contains two equal-length trajectories: 8K, 16K, and 32K packs comprise two 4K, 8K, and 16K trajectories, respectively. Each trajectory starts from an independent initial state. All measured steps commit state, while reads within a step use its incoming snapshot. Windows do not cross trajectory boundaries. Weights are randomly initialized and hidden-state inputs are synthetic, with fixed random seed 20261015; input hidden states have standard deviation 1.0, while initial states and backward cotangents have standard deviation 0.01. This workload measures the computation and activation costs of the memory branch.

Memory updates use a fixed chunked-WY implementation.

F.2 Measurement Method

Each pack length and window budget define a paired experiment. Both variants receive 5 warmups and 20 measured trials; successive pairs alternate between whole-pack→\rightarrowwindowed and windowed→\rightarrowwhole-pack order, yielding 240 measured samples. Each window budget has an independently measured whole-pack baseline, accounting for the small baseline-time differences between rows at the same length.

CUDA events measure forward-plus-backward (F+B) time, including block execution, inner products of the output and final state with fixed cotangents, and backward through the scalar objective. Input preparation, schedule construction, and compilation occur outside the timed region. Peak memory is PyTorch peak allocated, including block parameters, inputs and cotangents, outputs, gradients, and both prepared schedules. This metric measures live tensor allocations, distinct from memory reserved by the caching allocator. The main table reports medians; percentage changes are computed from unrounded medians.

F.3 Full Results

As pack length increases from 8K to 32K, whole-pack peak memory grows from 12.37 GiB to 47.83 GiB, while 4096-token windows grow from 8.36 GiB to 9.49 GiB. Windowing bounds the lifetime of projections and intermediates, while retained outputs and boundary states still grow with length. Across the three lengths, the median time increases for 4096-token windows are 15.0%, 11.1%, and 1.6%, respectively, showing that windowing overhead depends on the workload.

F.4 Measurement Variability

Table 16 reports medians, interquartile intervals [Q25, Q75], and sample standard deviations, all in ms.

All samples are retained, including whole-pack trials at 16K/2048 (378.03 ms) and 32K/2048 (562.40 ms), and a windowed trial at 32K/4096 (640.58 ms). The 1.6% reported in the chapter therefore describes the median time difference; individual trials exhibit variability.

Appendix G Case Studies

We present four examples from a long English conversation. They show how MemT-1.0-Nano uses its memory as the history grows.

MemT-1.0-Nano keeps one latent memory slot for each conversation. History enters the slot through commit operations. A commit reads the incoming turns and writes their content into the slot, and the original text is not carried forward. What the model can answer therefore depends on the writes. The examples below show this at four points in the conversation. The text inside each box is given exactly as the model produced it.

G.1 Example 1: Factual Recall at 4K

The question asks for three things: the city, the purpose of the trip, and who holds the sample book. The model gives all three. It also keeps the nearby details with their owners, so Ningbo, the red toolbox, and the blue badge do not move to Chen Wei. The colour of the sample book is not mentioned, which is correct because the question does not ask for it.

{promptbox}

History: 4,340 tokens / first 25 turns of the conversation

Turn 1 (user): I’m Lin Yao, and I coordinate exhibitions at Qinghe Studio. … I think I’d rather sit than go straight back out.

Turn 2 (user): … I went to Suzhou to set up an exhibition and left my blue sample book with my colleague Chen Wei for safekeeping. That was a past work visit, separate from the future exhibition I’m still arranging. …

Turn 3 (user): … There’s a note about Xu Cheng, another colleague: he lives in Ningbo, handles lighting, and has the red toolbox. …

[… 21 turns of unrelated conversation about drawing, cooking, and household objects …]

Question: Which city did I go to last week, and what was I doing there? Who should I ask to get back the sample book I handed over?

Answer: You went to **Suzhou** last week. You were there to **set up an exhibition**.

You should ask **Chen Wei** for the sample book.

G.2 Example 2: Abstention on Missing Information at 16K

The question asks for the user’s birthday. The conversation never mentions a birthday. The model reports this instead of inventing a date. The answer is only six tokens long, and its brevity is the point. The question invites the model to fill the gap, and this answer does not.

{promptbox}

History: 16,457 tokens / first 105 turns of the conversation

Turn 1 (user): I’m Lin Yao, and I coordinate exhibitions at Qinghe Studio. …

Turn 18 (user): … The cup beside me has cooled, and the tea leaves have collected along one edge because the table isn’t perfectly level. …

[… 87 further turns that stay on drawing, cooking, and walking outside, and never mention a birthday or an age …]

Turn 103 (user): I once bought a set of colored pencils and spent more time arranging them than using them. …

Turn 105 (user): I kept the stub. It was easier to hold sideways for broad marks … Sometimes a broken object is simply broken. …

Question: What month and day is my birthday again? If we haven’t talked about it, just say you don’t know.

Answer: I don’t know.

G.3 Example 3: Rule Application at 32K

The fictional page of the notebook gives two chained rules. A blue badge grants eligibility to book a room. Eligibility to book, together with completed registration, grants eligibility to collect a silver toolbox. The second rule therefore depends on both conditions. If the registration condition is dropped, the rule grants an entitlement that the text never gives. The answer below applies the chain correctly to both characters. It also keeps the two fictional colleagues apart, so Xu Cheng’s incomplete registration does not move to Chen Wei.

{promptbox}

History: 32,931 tokens / first 230 turns of the conversation

Turn 4 (user): … anyone with a blue badge is eligible to book Room 2. Anyone eligible to book Room 2 who has completed registration is eligible to collect a silver toolbox. There are no other eligibility rules. I mean eligibility only: being allowed to book or collect something doesn’t mean the person has actually done it.

Turn 5 (user): The fictional Chen Wei has a blue badge and has completed registration. The fictional Xu Cheng also has a blue badge but hasn’t completed registration yet. …

[… 224 turns in which the story is never revisited and neither the rules nor the characters’ circumstances are restated …]

Turn 229 (user): A description of the sound itself makes more sense to me. …

Turn 230 (user): The radio voice has become my favorite thing in this invented film. …

Question: Given the rules and what we discussed about each person, are Chen Wei and Xu Cheng each eligible to collect the toolbox now? Briefly explain why.

Answer: Based on the rules provided in the text:

* **Chen Wei:** Yes, he is eligible. He has a blue badge and has completed registration.

* **Xu Cheng:** No, he is not eligible. Although he has a blue badge, he has not completed registration.

G.4 Example 4: Tracking an Update at 64K

The exhibition is first set for Saturday at 3 p.m. in the East Hall. It is then officially changed to Sunday at 4 p.m. The venue, the admission price, and the contact person all stay the same. A move to Monday is also proposed, but it is never decided. A correct answer must report the change and leave the proposal out. The answer below does both. It answers the second half of the question by negation instead of repeating the values. The conversation runs for 508 more turns after the change, and the model still separates a settled change from a passing suggestion.

{promptbox}

History: 65,587 tokens / first 516 turns of the conversation

Turn 6 (user): The small exhibition I’m planning for the future was originally set for Saturday at 3 p.m. in the East Hall, with free admission, and Chen Wei is the contact person. … I’m waiting for the final timing decision before I send a notice, so the draft is still open.

Turn 7 (user): … the confirmation has just arrived too: the exhibition has officially changed to Sunday at 4 p.m. Everything else stays the same. This change is definite, so that’s the new arrangement. …

Turn 8 (user): … Someone has just suggested moving the exhibition to Monday, but I haven’t decided and haven’t announced another change. It’s only a suggestion under consideration, not a confirmed arrangement. …

[… 508 turns in which the exhibition is not raised again; the closing turns discuss a lamp, a book, and a patch of wall …]

Turn 514 (user): … The wall opposite has a little patch where the paint catches the light differently. …

Turn 516 (user): … My first glance supplies a shadow, then the second supplies the patch. …

Question: When was the exhibition originally scheduled, and what time was it officially changed to? Did the venue, admission price or contact person change?

Answer: The exhibition was originally scheduled for **Saturday at 3 p.m.** It was officially changed to **Sunday at 4 p.m.**

No, the venue, admission price, or contact person did not change. The change was solely to a different time on a different day.
